sections.b: From Latin praeter, "past." Most of the book was fulfilled in the first centuries: the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 and the conflict with pagan Rome. Partial preterists still expect a future return of Christ and resurrection (chapters 19–22). Full preterists believe even those were fulfilled, a view almost all churches reject. Early forms appear in Eusebius; the Jesuit scholar Luis de Alcázar (1614) gave it its modern shape. Its strength: it takes seriously that the book was written to real churches about things that would "soon take place" (1:1).

The book is a coded map of church history from John's day to the end, often using a "day for a year" rule, so 1,260 days become 1,260 years. Joachim of Fiore (1100s) began it; it became the standard Protestant view from the Reformation to the 1800s: Luther, Isaac Newton, Jonathan Edwards, Matthew Henry, and the founders of the Seventh-day Adventist church. Its weakness: its interpreters have never agreed on the map, and each tends to place the end in his own day.

sections.b: Chapters 4–22 describe events still to come: a tribulation, the Antichrist, Christ's return, and a 1,000-year reign. Early church writers such as Irenaeus and Hippolytus held a simple futurism. The Jesuit Francisco Ribera (1590) revived it. In the 1830s John Nelson Darby joined it to dispensationalism and a pre-tribulation rapture, and the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970) and the Left Behind novels (1995–2007) made it the most popular American view.

sections.b: The book is a symbolic picture of the battle between God and evil in every age, not a timeline. Its roots go back to Tyconius and Augustine (late 300s). Many modern scholars hold an "eclectic" view: the book spoke first to Rome, describes patterns that recur in every age, and points to a real future end. G. K. Beale and Craig Keener are examples.

sections.b: The preterist and futurist views were both shaped in the Counter-Reformation. Protestants said the pope was the beast and Rome was Babylon. Catholic scholars answered: Ribera put the beast in the far future, and Alcázar put it in the distant past. Either way, it was not the pope.

common: "Literal" readers are futurists, and everyone else "spiritualizes."
You have to pick one view.
uncommon: Every view reads some things literally and some symbolically; the question is which.
Many scholars combine all four: first-century meaning (preterist), recurring pattern (idealist), and final fulfillment (futurist).

claude.title: Ask which view the book itself models
claude.body: When Revelation explains its own symbols (1:20; 17:9–18), it always points to something in John's own world (churches, a city, kings) and never to a date. That favors reading it first through first-century eyes. But the book also insists on a real ending: a real return, real resurrection, a real new creation (19–22). My reading is that the book trains you to see your own Rome while waiting for the real end, which combines the preterist, idealist and futurist instincts in that order.

Visions and dreams; heavenly journeys; angel guides who explain what is seen; symbolic animals for empires; numbered periods of time; cosmic battles between good and evil; and a final judgment and new world. Most were written for people under pressure from great empires: Babylon, Persia, the Seleucid kings or Rome.

Most apocalypses claim to be written by an ancient hero such as Enoch, Ezra or Baruch. John uses his own name and writes to real churches he knows. Revelation is also a letter (1:4) and a prophecy (1:3), and it tells readers not to seal it up (22:10), unlike Daniel (Daniel 12:4). And its center is not a coming hero but a Lamb who has already been slaughtered and raised.

Symbols let writers say dangerous things about rulers without naming them, and they help readers see the spiritual reality behind events, the way a political cartoon shows what a photograph cannot. A modern reader who sees an eagle or a bear in a cartoon knows it means a nation; ancient readers knew that beasts meant empires.

common: "Apocalypse" means the end of the world.
uncommon: "Apocalypse" means an unveiling. The point is seeing clearly, not destruction.

The seventh seal opens into the seven trumpets, and the seventh trumpet into the seven bowls. Many futurists hold this.

sections.b: Each set covers the same period from a new angle, ending each time at the end, with growing intensity: a fourth (6:8), a third (8:7–12), then everything (16:3). Victorinus of Pettau, who wrote the oldest surviving commentary on Revelation around AD 260, taught this. Support: each seventh ends with thunder, lightning and an earthquake (8:5; 11:19; 16:18), getting bigger each time.

sections.b: Another way to see the shape: the book moves from seven real cities (2–3) to two symbolic ones, Babylon (17–18) and the new Jerusalem (21–22), introduced with the same words (17:1; 21:9). The reader is a citizen of one and is asked to choose.

common: Revelation is a strict timeline, chapter by chapter.
uncommon: Revelation may be more like a set of camera angles on the same events, each closer than the last.

claude.title: The three sevens follow the three layers of the tabernacle
claude.body: The seals begin at the altar outside (6:9), the trumpets begin at the gold incense altar inside the Holy Place (8:3; 9:13), and the bowls come straight out of the sanctuary itself, "the tent of the testimony," after the ark has been seen (11:19; 15:5–8). Each set moves one step deeper into God's house. That fits a recapitulation reading: the same history, judged from ever closer to God's presence. Scholars note the temple settings; reading them as a deliberate inward progression is my own proposal.

Every use outside 7:14 is about what churches were already facing or about to face.

The popular "seven-year tribulation" comes from Daniel's seventieth "week" (Daniel 9:24–27), joined to Revelation's 3½-year periods (11:2–3; 12:6; 13:5) and Jesus's words about "great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world" (Matthew 24:21). Revelation itself never says "seven years." Futurists see a gap of the whole church age between Daniel's 69th and 70th weeks; others see the 70th week fulfilled in Christ's ministry and the following years.

In Matthew 24, Mark 13 and Luke 21, Jesus speaks both of Jerusalem's destruction ("when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies," Luke 21:20) and of his coming. Preterists read the "great tribulation" as AD 66–70; futurists as a future period; many read both, the first as a preview of the second.

common: Christians will escape all end-time suffering.
uncommon: In Revelation the faithful are protected from God's wrath but not from the world's hostility. The martyrs "came out of" the great tribulation by going through it (7:14).

claude.title: "Kept from the hour" may mean kept through it
claude.body: The promise to Philadelphia uses tērēsō ek, "I will keep you out of" the hour of testing (3:10). John uses the same verb and preposition in only one other place in his writings: Jesus's prayer, "I am not asking you to take them out of the world, but to keep them from the evil one" (John 17:15). There, "keep from" explicitly does not mean "remove." This has been noted by post-tribulation writers such as Robert Gundry; I find it the strongest single word study on the question.

sections.b: 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17 (caught up to meet the Lord in the air), 1 Corinthians 15:51–52 (changed at the last trumpet), John 14:2–3 ("I will come back and take you to be with me"), and Matthew 24:40–41 ("one will be taken and the other left").

Most of church history expected one return of Christ, with believers rising to meet him as he comes. The idea of a separate, earlier, secret rapture before a tribulation was developed by John Nelson Darby in the 1830s, among the Plymouth Brethren in Britain. It spread through the Niagara Bible Conferences, the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), Dallas Theological Seminary, Hal Lindsey's books and the Left Behind series. Some find earlier hints, such as a sermon attributed to Pseudo-Ephraem (perhaps 500s) and the Baptist Morgan Edwards (1788).

Revelation never uses the word for the church. Its only "caught up" (harpazō) is the male child, Jesus, snatched up to God's throne (12:5). Readers see the rapture pictured at 4:1 (pre-tribulation), 11:12 (mid-tribulation), 14:14–16 (the grain harvest), or at Christ's return in 19:11–14. The word "church" disappears after chapter 3, which pre-tribulation writers take as a sign the church is gone; others note that "God's people," "saints" and "servants" appear throughout.

"Meet" in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 (apantēsis) was the word for a city's leaders going out to welcome a visiting king or general and escorting him back into the city. Many scholars think that means believers rise to welcome Jesus as he comes to earth, not to leave with him.

common: The rapture is clearly described in Revelation 4:1.
The pre-tribulation rapture is the historic Christian view.
uncommon: The rapture and the second coming are one event, with believers rising to welcome the returning king.

claude.title: Revelation’s model of "going up" is the Lamb’s own path
claude.body: The only person caught up in Revelation is the Son (12:5), and the only people who go up to heaven are the two witnesses, after faithful witness, death and resurrection (11:7–12). The 144,000 "follow the Lamb wherever he goes" (14:4). My reading: Revelation frames the hope as following Jesus's own path (witness, suffering, vindication, ascension) rather than escaping before trouble. That is closest to post-tribulation and idealist readings.

Christ returns before a literal 1,000-year reign on earth. This was the view of many early writers: Papias, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus, who imagined a world of astonishing abundance. Historic premillennialism (George Ladd) sees one people of God; dispensational premillennialism sees the millennium fulfilling promises to national Israel, with a rebuilt temple.

The thousand years is the present age between Christ's two comings. Satan was bound by Christ's victory (Matthew 12:29; Luke 10:18), and the saints reign with Christ now in heaven. Augustine made this the standard view (City of God 20.7–9), after first holding a premillennial view himself; it is held by Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and many Reformed churches.

Christ returns after a long golden age brought about by the spread of the gospel. Popular among Puritans and 1800s American Protestants (Jonathan Edwards, Charles Hodge), it fueled missions and social reform. It faded after the world wars, though some still hold it.

Expectations of a thousand-year kingdom have inspired movements both peaceful and violent. In 1534–35 radical Anabaptists seized the city of Münster, declared it the New Jerusalem, and were crushed. In the 1600s the English Fifth Monarchy Men expected Christ's reign soon. Historians use "millenarian" for any movement that expects a coming perfect age.

common: The Bible clearly teaches a future 1,000-year reign.
uncommon: The doctrine rests mostly on one chapter of symbolic writing. Everyone, premillennial or not, reads some of chapter 20 symbolically (a chain that binds a spirit, a key, an abyss).

claude.title: Isaiah 24 may be the blueprint for Revelation 20
claude.body: Isaiah 24:21–23 describes the powers of heaven and the kings of earth gathered "like prisoners in a pit," shut up "and after many days punished," followed by the Lord reigning "on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem" in glory. That is the sequence of Revelation 20: bound in a pit, a long period, a release and punishment, and God's reign in his city. Premillennial writers cite Isaiah 24:22. My suggestion is that the whole shape of Revelation 20, not just the prison, is modeled on Isaiah 24–25, which also gives us "he will swallow up death forever" and "God will wipe away tears" (Isaiah 25:8), both used in Revelation 21:4. If so, John is reading Isaiah's "many days" as his "thousand years," a long but symbolic period.

sections.b: The return of Jesus is the book's frame. It opens with "Look! He is coming with the clouds" (1:7) and closes with "Yes, I am coming soon" (22:20). In between, "coming" is used in several ways.

sections.b: Darkened sun and moon, earthquakes, people hiding in rocks, a day of wrath (Isaiah 2:10–21; Isaiah 13:9–10; Joel 2:1–11, 31; Zephaniah 1:14–18). Many of these "days" came in history: Isaiah 13 uses cosmic language for the fall of Babylon to the Medes, and Isaiah 34 for the judgment of Edom. That is why preterists read Revelation's cosmic signs as the collapse of nations, while futurists expect literal signs in the sky.

sections.b: "The great day of their anger" (6:17), "the great day of God, the All-Powerful" (16:14). The prophets' day of the Lord was also a day of rescue: "Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved" (Joel 2:32), which Peter quoted at Pentecost (Acts 2:21).

A different phrase: kyriakē hēmera, "the day belonging to the Lord." Early Christians used it for Sunday, the day of the resurrection (Didache 14:1; Ignatius, To the Magnesians 9:1). A few interpreters, such as E. W. Bullinger, read 1:10 as "I was in the Spirit [transported into] the day of the Lord," the end times; most think John simply says when the vision came.

sections.h: How it works in the book
sections.b: Wrath answers the martyrs' cry, "How long, Sovereign Lord... until you judge?" (6:10). It falls on those who "destroy the earth" (11:18) and who shed the blood of God's people (16:6). The plagues are paired with repeated calls to repent (9:20–21; 16:9, 11). In the songs, God's judgments are called "true and just" (15:3; 16:7; 19:2).

sections.b: A deliberate shock (6:16). Lambs are not angry. The one who judges is the one who was slaughtered for the people he judges, which means his anger cannot be selfish.

Theologians who have lived through war, such as Miroslav Volf from the former Yugoslavia, have argued that belief in God's final judgment is what frees victims from taking revenge themselves. Revelation's martyrs ask God to judge; they never pick up a sword. Christians who follow the Lamb "conquer" by testimony (12:11).

common: God's wrath in Revelation is arbitrary destruction.
uncommon: Several bowls give back what was done: those who poured out blood are given blood to drink (16:6). Some scholars describe the plagues as God handing people over to what they chose (compare Romans 1:24–28).

sections.b: Does Revelation see one people of God or two? This question shapes how you read chapters 7, 11, 12, 14, 20 and 21. The study page collects every note on the question.

sections.b: The word "church" appears 19 times in chapters 1–3 and then not again until 22:16. The 144,000 are listed tribe by tribe (7:4–8). Jerusalem is central (11:8; 20:9). Paul expects a future turning of Israel: "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:25–26).

The church is called "a kingdom and priests" (1:6; 5:10), Israel's own title (Exodus 19:6). John hears 144,000 from Israel and then sees a crowd from every nation (7:4, 9). One bride (19:7). One city, with the tribes on the gates and the apostles on the foundations (21:12–14). Paul: "If you belong to Christ, you are Abraham's offspring" (Galatians 3:29).

sections.b: Reading "synagogue of Satan" (2:9; 3:9) or Babylon as "the Jews" has been used to fuel hatred. In context these are local disputes inside the Jewish and Christian community of Asia, written by a Jewish author who loved Israel's Scriptures. After the Holocaust, many churches officially rejected readings that blame or erase the Jewish people.

common: You must choose between "replacement theology" and "two peoples."
uncommon: Many positions in between hold that Israel is neither replaced nor kept separate, but enlarged.

claude.title: One olive tree, with Israel at the root
claude.body: Revelation never "replaces" Israel: it names the tribes one by one and writes them on the gates of the final city. But it also never keeps two separate peoples in the final picture: one bride, one city, one Lamb. My reading is closest to Paul's single olive tree (Romans 11:17–24): Israel is the trunk and the nations are grafted in. You enter through Israel's names (21:12) and stand on the apostles' (21:14).

Irenaeus (about AD 180) and Hippolytus (about 200) were already combining these into one end-time figure.

The model for many of these was Antiochus IV "Epiphanes" ("god made visible"), who set up a pagan altar in the Jerusalem temple in 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54). The Ascension of Isaiah, a Christian writing from about John's time, says the devil Beliar will come "in the form of a man, a lawless king, the murderer of his mother," clearly Nero (Ascension of Isaiah 4:2). The Didache warns that "the world-deceiver will appear as a son of God" (16:4).
Nero; Domitian; Muhammad (medieval Christians); various popes (Reformers); Napoleon; Mussolini; Hitler; Stalin; and many modern politicians. Every confident identification so far has been wrong.

common: Revelation describes "the Antichrist" by name.
uncommon: John's own letters define antichrist as a spirit of denial already at work, not only a single future ruler.

claude.title: Look for the counterfeit, not the person
claude.body: John's letters say the antichrist spirit "denies that Jesus came in the flesh" (1 John 4:2–3). Revelation's beast is a counterfeit Lamb: slaughtered-and-healed (13:3), worshiped, given authority by its "father" the dragon (13:2, 4). Reading both together, I think John cares less about naming one man than about training readers to spot any power that imitates Christ's death and resurrection to claim worship. That makes the warning permanent rather than only future.

sections.b: The word was used for the emperor's image stamped on coins, for official seals on contracts and bills of sale, and for brands on animals and slaves. Every coin in a Christian's purse carried the emperor's image and titles, sometimes "son of the divine." Some historians link the mark to the imperial cult: trade guilds in Asia held feasts honoring the emperor and local gods, and refusing could cost a person their livelihood.

God's servants are sealed "on their foreheads" (7:3) and carry the Lamb's and Father's name there (14:1; 22:4). The Shema told Israel to bind God's words "on your hand" and "between your eyes" (Deuteronomy 6:8), which observant Jews still do with tefillin. The high priest wore "Holy to the LORD" on his forehead (Exodus 28:36–38). The mark of the beast is the opposite of all three.

Social Security numbers, credit cards, barcodes, RFID chips, vaccines, and digital IDs have all been proposed. The KJV's "in their right hand" (Greek epi, "on") helped the implant idea. Each new technology has drawn the same fear.

common: The mark is a technology that someone could take by accident.
uncommon: Every person in Revelation is marked by someone. The mark is about whom you worship (14:9–11), so no one takes it by accident.

claude.title: The mark is a counterfeit priesthood
claude.body: In Revelation every believer becomes a priest (1:6; 5:10; 20:6), and the priest's mark was on the forehead (Exodus 28:36–38). The final promise is "his name will be on their foreheads" (22:4). Since the beast's mark is also on the forehead, I read it as a rival priesthood: people who serve and represent the beast in daily life. That explains why it is tied to buying and selling, the daily "liturgy" of empire.

sections.b: In Hebrew and Greek, letters were also numbers, so any name had a number. A graffito in Pompeii reads "I love her whose number is 545." The Sibylline Oracles give Jesus's name the number 888 (Iēsous: 10 + 8 + 200 + 70 + 400 + 200), one more than seven three times over, against the beast's one less. In Hebrew letters, Nero Caesar (נרון קסר) adds to 666; the Latin spelling (נרו קסר) adds to 616, the number in some manuscripts. See the page on Nero.

Papyrus 115 (about AD 300), the oldest copy of this verse, and Codex Ephraemi read 616. Irenaeus knew both and defended 666 as found in "all the most approved and ancient copies" (Against Heresies 5.30.1).

With enough flexibility in spelling and system, almost any name can be made to reach 666, which is why the Nero solution is valued: it uses ordinary Hebrew spelling and explains the 616 variant.

Six falls short of seven, so 666 is "always falling short." It is also a triangular number (the sum of 1 to 36), and 36 is itself the sum of 1 to 8, which some link to the beast as "an eighth" king (17:11). Some link it to the 666 talents of gold that came to Solomon each year (1 Kings 10:14).

common: 666 is a code for a future person we must decode.
uncommon: The first readers likely could decode it, because John says they could.

claude.title: 666 and the king who broke the king’s law
claude.body: 1 Kings 10 is the chapter with 666 talents. It goes on to list exactly what Deuteronomy 17:16–17 forbade a king of Israel to pile up: gold, horses from Egypt, and (in chapter 11) many wives. It describes Solomon controlling the horse and chariot trade (1 Kings 10:28–29), just as the beast controls buying and selling (13:17). My speculation: "the number of a man" points to the moment a king of God's own people turned into a Pharaoh. The beast is what power becomes when it grasps at wealth, weapons and control.

Ezēsan, "they lived" or "they came to life." The same verb is used of Jesus's resurrection in 2:8 ("who died and came to life") and of the beast's recovery in 13:14. Premillennialists argue it must mean bodily resurrection in 20:4 because it plainly does in 20:5 ("the rest of the dead did not come to life"). Amillennialists answer that John pairs a first and second resurrection with a first and second death, and the first death is physical while the second is not.

John sees "the souls of those who had been beheaded because of their testimony about Jesus" and those who had not worshiped the beast (20:4). Beheading was the Roman punishment for citizens and the method of execution tradition gives for Paul. The thrones and judgment come from Daniel 7:9, 22: "judgment was given in favor of the holy people."
"Blessed and holy" (20:6) is the fifth of Revelation's seven blessings. They will be "priests of God and of Christ," fulfilling 1:6 and 5:10.

"White" is the color of purity and victory throughout the book. "Earth and sky fled from his presence, and there was no place for them" (20:11) clears the stage: nothing stands between the judge and the judged. The sea, Death and Hades all give up their dead (20:13): no one is lost, and no one escapes.

"Books" record deeds; "the book of life" records names (20:12, 15). The picture comes from Daniel 7:10 ("the court was seated, and the books were opened"). Malachi speaks of "a scroll of remembrance" (Malachi 3:16), and a psalm asks God to record tears in his book (Psalm 56:8). Revelation holds both: deeds matter, and belonging to the Lamb matters most (13:8; 21:27).

sections.b: Many readers ask how judgment "by what they had done" fits salvation by grace. Paul says the same two things: God "will repay each person according to what they have done" (Romans 2:6), and "it is by grace you have been saved... not by works" (Ephesians 2:8–9). Jesus's parable of the sheep and goats judges by deeds of mercy (Matthew 25:31–46). Most traditions say deeds are the evidence of what a person has become, and the book of life is the ground of rescue.

John says "him who was seated on it" (20:11), normally God the Father. Elsewhere the New Testament says the Father "has entrusted all judgment to the Son" (John 5:22; 2 Corinthians 5:10). By 22:1 the throne is "the throne of God and of the Lamb."

The last judgment has been painted and carved more than almost any other scene: over the doors of medieval churches (Autun, Conques), by Giotto in Padua (about 1305), and by Michelangelo on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel (1536–41).
The final destination of the beast, the false prophet, the devil, Death and Hades, and those not found in the book of life (19:20; 20:10, 14–15; 21:8). discusses the views in more depth.

Gehenna, the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem where children had been sacrificed to Molech (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31–32), became Jesus's word for the place of final judgment (Matthew 5:22; Mark 9:43–48). 1 Enoch speaks of an abyss "full of fire" for the fallen angels (1 Enoch 90:24–26).

The lake of fire in the underworld

The Egyptian Book of the Dead (spell 126) and tomb paintings show a lake of fire in the underworld, guarded by four baboons, which burns the wicked and refreshes the righteous. Greek myth had Pyriphlegethon, a river of fire in Hades. There is no evidence John borrowed from Egypt; fire as the picture of final judgment was common across the ancient world and already present in the Old Testament.

Jewish tradition says that on Rosh Hashanah three books are opened: one for the righteous, one for the wicked, and one for those in between (Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 16b). The traditional greeting for the season is "May you be inscribed in the book of life." Revelation's "books were opened" belongs to the same picture.

Calvinists stress God's choice before creation; Arminians stress that names can be "blotted out" (3:5; Exodus 32:33) and that the promise is to "the one who wins."
KJV 22:19 says "book of life" where nearly every Greek manuscript says "tree of life," because of Erasmus's back-translation from Latin in 1516.

"Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more" (21:1), quoting Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. The Bible ends where it began: with heaven, earth, a garden, a river and a tree.

Kainos, "new," often means new in quality rather than brand new. Some read total replacement: "the heavens will disappear with a roar; the elements will be destroyed by fire" (2 Peter 3:10–12). But the oldest manuscripts of 2 Peter 3:10 end with "the earth and everything done in it will be laid bare" (found, exposed), not "burned up." Many read renewal: creation "will be liberated from its bondage to decay" (Romans 8:19–23). "I am making everything new" (21:5) says everything new, not new things.

The garden becomes a city, but the garden is still inside it: a river (Genesis 2:10; Revelation 22:1), the tree of life (Genesis 2:9; Revelation 22:2), gold and precious stones (Genesis 2:12; Revelation 21:18–21), God walking with people (Genesis 3:8; Revelation 21:3), and the curse removed (Genesis 3:17; Revelation 22:3).

uncommon: Revelation's final scene is God moving in with humanity on a renewed earth.

sections.b: In Asia, people were asked to honor the emperor as "lord and god." Pergamum even had a choir of "hymn singers of the god Augustus" who sang at imperial festivals. Revelation's songs give the emperors' titles only to God and the Lamb: "You are worthy, our Lord and God" (4:11). Choosing whom to worship is the book's central decision (13:4, 8; 14:7, 9).
The gold bowls of incense "are the prayers of God's people" (5:8). In 8:3–5 those prayers go up and fire comes down: prayer moves history.

claude.title: Silence is the answer to "How long?"
claude.body: The martyrs ask "How long?" (6:10). After the sixth seal, heaven falls silent for half an hour (8:1), then incense with "the prayers of all God's people" rises (8:3–4). In the temple, incense was offered while the people prayed outside (Luke 1:10), and later Jewish tradition says the angels' singing stopped so Israel's prayers could be heard. My reading: the silence is heaven pausing everything to listen to the martyrs, and the trumpets are the answer. The incense link is noted by Bauckham; the half-hour as a deliberate "listening" pause is my emphasis.

sections.b: Jesus is "the faithful witness" (1:5; 3:14). Antipas is "my faithful witness, who was killed" (2:13). Martyrs are under the altar (6:9), the two witnesses are killed (11:7), Babylon is "drunk with the blood of the witnesses to Jesus" (17:6), and the saints win "by the word of their testimony" and by not loving their lives (12:11). Those beheaded "because of their testimony" reign with Christ (20:4).

They are told to "rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants... was complete" (6:11), a hard word that expects more suffering before the end.

Tertullian, about AD 197, wrote to Roman officials: "The more you mow us down, the more we grow; the blood of Christians is seed" (Apology 50). That is very close to Revelation's logic: witnesses die and are vindicated, and their death converts where plagues could not (11:11–13).

Some scholars think Revelation expects widespread martyrdom; others note it names only one martyr (Antipas) and is warning about what faithfulness may cost. Roman persecution was mostly local and occasional until the empire-wide campaigns of Decius (250) and Diocletian (303–311).

More calls to repent go to churches than to the world. The book’s first audience is the church.

In the Old Testament the word is shuv, "turn back," the word of every prophet: "Turn back, turn back from your evil ways! Why will you die, people of Israel?" (Ezekiel 33:11). The Greek word adds "change of mind." In Revelation repentance always involves a concrete change: "do the works you did at first" (2:5).

The trumpets strike only a third, and the narrator twice notes that people "still did not turn away" (9:20–21). The judgments are meant to bring people back. Even Jezebel was given "time to repent" (2:21).

Yes, once: after the two witnesses rise, the survivors "were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven" (11:13), the very response the first angel calls for in 14:7. Richard Bauckham argues this is the book's turning point: witness converts where plagues could not. In the earthquake only a tenth of the city falls and 7,000 die, a reversal of Elijah's story where 7,000 were spared and the rest perished (1 Kings 19:18).

sections.b: C. S. Lewis called Jesus's saying "this generation will certainly not pass away until all these things have happened" (Mark 13:30) "the most embarrassing verse in the Bible" (The World's Last Night, 1960), and he took it seriously rather than explaining it away. Revelation's "soon" raises the same question.

Preterist: soon meant soon; much happened in the first century. Futurist: "quickly once it begins," or soon by God's measure: "With the Lord a day is like a thousand years... The Lord is not slow in keeping his promise... he is patient with you" (2 Peter 3:8–9). Idealist: every generation stands near the end, because the decisive victory (the cross) is already won. Some point out that Daniel was told to seal his book because the end was far (Daniel 12:4, 9), while John is told not to seal his (22:10).

Whatever "soon" means for dates, it means urgency for choices: "Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy" (22:7). The book's response to "I am coming soon" is not calculation but prayer: "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus" (22:20).

In 9 BC the cities of Asia changed their calendar so the year began on Augustus's birthday. An inscription from Priene, near Ephesus, says the birthday of "the god" was "the beginning of the good news (euangelia) for the world." Christians proclaimed a different "good news" about a different Son of God.

Not worshiping meant skipping city festivals and trade-guild meals, which looked disloyal and could cost work. Pliny's letter to Trajan (about AD 112) describes Christians in nearby Bithynia brought to trial; those who refused to offer incense and wine to the emperor's image and curse Christ were executed (Letters 10.96). Pliny notes that "those who are really Christians cannot be forced" to do these things.

The land beast enforces worship of the sea beast and its image (13:12–15). The songs give "worthy," "Lord and God," and "Savior" to God alone, titles used of emperors. The question "Who is like the beast?" (13:4) parodies Israel's song, "Who is like you, LORD, among the gods?" (Exodus 15:11).

The beast "conquers" the saints by killing them (13:7), and in the same act they conquer the beast (15:2). The Lamb "has won the victory" (5:5) by being slaughtered.

Nike, the winged goddess of victory, was everywhere in the Roman world: on coins, monuments and military standards. Emperors celebrated victories with parades and arches. Athletes who won at the games received wreaths (stephanoi), the word Revelation uses for "crowns" (2:10; 3:11). John takes the empire's favorite word and redefines it.

Irenaeus (about AD 180), who knew Polycarp, who knew John, says the vision was seen "toward the end of Domitian's reign" (Against Heresies 5.30.3). The churches seem well established, and the imperial cult in Asia matches the 80s–90s. Most scholars hold this date.

John measures a temple that seems still standing (11:1–2). The seven kings could make the sixth king Nero or Galba. Preterists like Kenneth Gentry argue for this date, and it was common among scholars in the 1800s.

sections.h: Who did early Christians think he was?
sections.b:

John the apostle, son of Zebedee, was the view of Justin and Irenaeus and of most of the church through history. John the Elder, a different leader in Asia mentioned by Papias (quoted in Eusebius, Church History 3.39.4), was proposed by Dionysius. Another prophet named John, otherwise unknown, is the view of many modern scholars. All agree he was a Jewish Christian prophet with deep knowledge of the Old Testament and close ties to the churches of Asia.

Dionysius noticed that Revelation's Greek is rough and very different from the Gospel of John, though the two share key words like "Lamb," "Word," "witness" and "living water." Revelation's grammar sometimes breaks the normal rules, for example "from the one who is" in 1:4, where the Greek keeps God's name in the subject form even after "from." Many scholars think this is deliberate, showing respect for the divine name (compare Exodus 3:14), or the Greek of a man who thought in Hebrew or Aramaic.

Because of its authorship and its use by groups predicting the end, Revelation was slow to be accepted in the Eastern churches. Some Greek lists of Scripture leave it out, and it is still not read in the Orthodox Sunday lectionary. In the West it was accepted early. At the Reformation, Luther wrote in 1522 that his "spirit cannot accommodate itself to this book," though he softened this later; Zwingli doubted it, and Calvin wrote commentaries on every New Testament book except Revelation (and 2 and 3 John).
John calls his book "prophecy" seven times and is told "you must prophesy again" (10:11). He stands in line with Ezekiel and Daniel, receiving visions, eating a scroll, and being told what to write.

sections.h: God’s features on a human figure
sections.b: In Daniel 7, the "one like a son of man" comes to the Ancient of Days, whose hair is white like wool. In Revelation 1, the son of man himself has the white hair. John fuses the two figures: Jesus shares God's identity. This is one of the earliest and boldest statements of Jesus's divinity in the New Testament, made by picture rather than by argument.

"Son of Man" is the title Jesus used for himself most often in the Gospels, about eighty times. Before the high priest he said, "You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Mighty One and coming on the clouds of heaven" (Mark 14:62). In Jewish writings of the time, especially the part of 1 Enoch called the Similitudes (chapters 37–71), the Son of Man was a heavenly judge hidden before creation. 4 Ezra 13 pictures "something like a man" rising from the sea and flying with the clouds.

In 14:14 "one like a son of man" sits on a white cloud with a gold crown and a sharp sickle, reaping the earth. Most readers take him as Christ gathering his people; a few, noting that an angel gives him orders (14:15), think he is an angel.

Arnion, "lamb," is Revelation's main name for Jesus: 29 uses, 28 of them for Christ. The other one is the land beast, which has horns "like a lamb" (13:11). The whole book can be read as the story of how a slaughtered lamb rules the world.

sections.b: An elder announces "the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David" (5:5, from Genesis 49:9 and Isaiah 11:1, 10), and John turns and sees a Lamb "that looked as if it had been slaughtered" (5:6). John hears one thing and sees another, and the second explains the first. The book redefines power: the Messiah wins by dying.

The Passover lamb (Exodus 12), whose blood marked the doors and freed Israel from Egypt; Revelation's plagues and song of Moses keep this in view. The lamb led to slaughter (Isaiah 53:7). "The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29, though John's Gospel uses a different Greek word, amnos).

The Lamb has "seven horns and seven eyes" (5:6): all power and all sight, from Zechariah's "seven eyes of the LORD that range throughout the earth" (Zechariah 4:10). A horned, fighting lamb was not new: in 1 Enoch's "Animal Apocalypse" the Jewish people are sheep, and a ram with a great horn leads them in battle (1 Enoch 90:9–12). John keeps the battle but changes the weapon: this lamb has been slaughtered.

claude.title: Twenty-eight is four sevens
claude.body: Richard Bauckham noted that "Lamb" is used for Christ exactly 28 times, 7 × 4: seven for completeness, four for the world. I counted in the Greek text and found the same: 29 uses of arnion, one of which (13:11) is the beast. If the count is intended, John is saying in numbers what he says in words: the Lamb's victory is complete and worldwide.

sections.b: "The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches" (1:20). They may be guardian angels, or human messengers or leaders. Each letter scolds its angel for the church's sins, which suggests the angel and the church share one identity.

"The seven angels who stand before God" (8:2) recall Raphael's words in Tobit 12:15: "I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who stand ready and enter before the glory of the Lord." 1 Enoch 20 names seven archangels: Uriel, Raphael, Raguel, Michael, Sariel, Gabriel and Remiel. Revelation names only Michael (12:7) and Abaddon/Apollyon, the angel of the abyss (9:11).

The angel of chapter 10 is "wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head; his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire" (10:1). Some readers think he is Christ himself, since these are the features of the son of man (1:15–16) and of God's throne (4:3). Most think he is a great angel reflecting Christ's glory.

Twice John falls down to worship an angel and is stopped: "Don't do that! I am a servant with you and with your brothers and sisters... Worship God!" (19:10; 22:8–9). Some early Christians were tempted to worship angels (Colossians 2:18), and some Jewish writings show the same caution.
Around God's throne are four zōa, "living ones," like a lion, an ox, a human and an eagle, each with six wings and covered with eyes (4:6–8). They never stop saying, "Holy, holy, holy."

Many read them as all living creation worshiping God: wild animals, tame animals, humans and birds. A Jewish saying, recorded later, calls these four the mightiest of their kinds: the lion among wild beasts, the ox among tame ones, the eagle among birds, and humanity over all. In Revelation they also call out the four horsemen ("Come!" 6:1–7) and hand the bowls to the angels (15:7): creation itself takes part in judging those who destroy it (11:18).

From Irenaeus and Jerome on, Christian art gave them to the Gospel writers. The usual pairing is Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the ox and John the eagle. You can see them in medieval Bibles, church windows and the Book of Kells.
The KJV calls them "four beasts," the same word it uses for the monster of chapter 13, though the Greek words differ (zōa versus thērion). Modern translations say "living creatures."

claude.title: Israel’s camp around the throne
claude.body: In the wilderness Israel camped in four groups around the tabernacle (Numbers 2). Medieval Jewish tradition (for example Ibn Ezra, and Numbers Rabbah 2:7) gives the lead tribes banners: Judah a lion, Reuben a man, Ephraim an ox, Dan an eagle. If those banners are older than the written sources, the throne room is Israel's camp around God, and "the Lion of the tribe of Judah" (5:5) is named right beside the lion-faced creature. The banner tradition is written down later than Revelation, so this is a possible echo, not a proof.

The whole people of God: 12 tribes plus 12 apostles, which matches the city's 12 gates and 12 foundations (21:12–14). Angels who lead heavenly worship; one acts as an interpreter, the way angels do in Daniel (7:13). The raptured church in heaven, crowned and seated (many dispensationalists). A heavenly council like the one in Isaiah 24:23, "before his elders, gloriously."

David divided the priests into 24 divisions to serve in turn (1 Chronicles 24:7–19), and the temple musicians into 24 groups who "prophesied with harps" (1 Chronicles 25:1–31). The elders hold harps and bowls of incense, which are exactly the tasks of musicians and priests.

In the KJV the elders sing that Christ "hast redeemed us to God... and hast made us unto our God kings and priests" (5:9–10). The oldest manuscripts read "them," not "us." If "us" is right, the elders are redeemed humans; if "them" is right, they may be angels singing about humans. Most modern translations follow "them."

Their crowns are victory wreaths (stephanoi). Laying them before the throne echoes the way kings submitted to Rome: the Armenian king Tiridates laid his diadem before Nero's statue (Tacitus, Annals 15.29). Every honor they have, they hand back to God.
The archangel who leads heaven's armies and throws the dragon out of heaven (12:7–9). His name is a question: Mi-ka-el, "Who is like God?"

Daniel calls him "one of the chief princes" and "the great prince who protects your people," who will arise in a time of distress like no other (Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1). Jude 9 has him disputing with the devil over Moses's body, a story from a lost Jewish book called the Assumption of Moses. Paul's "voice of the archangel" at Christ's return (1 Thessalonians 4:16) may refer to him.

1 Enoch lists him among seven archangels, set over Israel (1 Enoch 20:5). In the Dead Sea Scrolls' War Scroll, God raises up "the dominion of Michael" among the angels and the kingdom of Israel among people for the final battle against darkness (1QM 17:6–7). Revelation 12 draws on this hope.

sections.h: When was the war in heaven?
sections.b: Readers disagree. (1) At the beginning, when Satan first rebelled; this is the version popularized by Milton's Paradise Lost. (2) At Jesus's death and exaltation: the war follows the child being "snatched up to God" (12:5), and the victory song says "now the salvation... has come" because the saints won "by the blood of the Lamb" (12:10–11); compare Jesus's words "I saw Satan fall like lightning" (Luke 10:18) and "now the ruler of this world will be driven out" (John 12:31). (3) In the future, in the middle of the tribulation (many futurists).

Jehovah's Witnesses identify Michael with the pre-human Christ, whom they see as a created being. Seventh-day Adventists also use "Michael" as a name for Christ, but affirm that he is fully God and not an angel. Most Christians see Michael as an angel acting because of the Lamb's victory.

Michael became the most honored angel in Christian devotion: Mont-Saint-Michel in France and Saint Michael's Mount in England, countless churches, and the Catholic "Prayer to Saint Michael" composed under Pope Leo XIII in 1886.

sections.b: Red, with seven heads and seven royal crowns and ten horns (12:3). The crowns sit on his heads, not his horns (the sea beast has them on its horns, 13:1): he claims to be king. Red may stand for murder: Jesus called the devil "a murderer from the beginning" (John 8:44). His tail sweeps a third of the stars to the earth (12:4), like the arrogant horn in Daniel 8:10.

The serpent of Eden (Genesis 3), and the promise that the woman's offspring would crush its head (Genesis 3:15). Leviathan, "the twisting serpent," the "dragon of the sea" (Isaiah 27:1; Psalm 74:13–14). Pharaoh as "the great dragon lying in his rivers" (Ezekiel 29:3). The ancient combat myths of a sea monster defeated by a god (see "End-times stories from other traditions").

He waits to devour the child (12:4), loses the war in heaven (12:7–9), is thrown down to earth "filled with fury, because he knows his time is short" (12:12), pursues the woman (12:13–17), gives his power to the beast (13:2), sends out frog-like spirits to gather the kings (16:13), is bound for a thousand years (20:2–3), is released, deceives the nations again, and is thrown into the lake of fire forever (20:7–10).

Leopard body, bear's feet, lion's mouth, ten crowned horns, seven heads (13:1–2): all four of Daniel's beasts rolled into one (Daniel 7:3–8). Daniel says his beasts are kingdoms (Daniel 7:17, 23). Its first referent is almost certainly Rome; futurists add a final world empire and ruler.

The beast's heads carry "blasphemous names" (13:1). Roman emperors took titles like divi filius ("son of a god"), Sebastos ("one to be worshiped," the Greek for Augustus), "Savior" and "Lord." Domitian liked to be addressed as "our lord and god" (Suetonius, Domitian 13). Coins and inscriptions in Asia carried these titles everywhere.

One head was "slaughtered" but healed (13:3), the same Greek as the Lamb "slaughtered" (5:6). The beast copies the death and resurrection of Christ. Many link this to the Nero legend (see Nero); others to the empire's near-collapse in the civil wars of AD 68–69, after which it revived under Vespasian. The Roman poet Juvenal called Domitian "a bald Nero" (Satires 4.38).

It "once was, now is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss" (17:8), a parody of God "who is, who was, and who is coming" (1:4). Its seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings (17:9–10), and its ten horns are ten kings who will turn on the prostitute (17:16).

The beast was Rome, and stands for every empire like it.

sections.b: Deuteronomy 13:1–3: a prophet who gives a sign that comes true but leads people to other gods is still false. Jesus warned, "False messiahs and false prophets will appear and perform great signs and wonders to deceive, if possible, even the elect" (Matthew 24:24). Paul speaks of the lawless one coming "with all kinds of counterfeit miracles" (2 Thessalonians 2:9).

In Asia, the provincial council and local elites built emperor temples, paid for festivals and served as high priests of the cult. They made worship of the emperor a civic duty. Talking statues and faked wonders were well known. Lucian describes Alexander of Abonoteichus, a "false prophet" of the 100s AD, who made a tame snake with a puppet head called Glycon that gave oracles through a hidden tube (Alexander the False Prophet). Christian stories said Simon Magus made statues walk.

It looks like the Lamb and sounds like the dragon. Jesus warned of "false prophets who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves" (Matthew 7:15). The danger is not obvious evil but religion that serves power.

sections.b: "These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth" (11:4) quotes Zechariah 4:3, 11–14, where two olive trees feed a lampstand. In Zechariah they are Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, a king and a priest. Revelation's witnesses are "a kingdom and priests" (1:6) in action.

They witness, are killed in "the great city... where their Lord was also crucified" (11:8), lie dead in public for three days, are raised by "the breath of life from God" (Ezekiel 37:10), and go up in a cloud while their enemies watch (Acts 1:9). Then "the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven" (11:13): their death does what the plagues could not.

claude.title: Israel and the church as the two branches
claude.body: Zechariah 4 has two olive trees feeding one lampstand; Romans 11 has one olive tree with natural branches (Israel) and grafted branches (the nations). Revelation 11 has two olive trees and two lampstands. My speculation: the two lampstands are believing Israel and the church from the nations, witnessing side by side as "a kingdom and priests" (1:6). That would explain why there are two, why they share one story of death and resurrection, and why they appear in Jerusalem. I have not found this in the major commentaries.

sections.b: Joseph dreamed that the sun, moon and eleven stars bowed to him, meaning Jacob, Rachel and his brothers (Genesis 37:9): sun, moon and twelve stars are the family of Israel. The prophets picture Zion as a woman in labor: "Before she goes into labor, she gives birth" (Isaiah 66:7–8); "Writhe in agony, Daughter Zion, like a woman in labor" (Micah 4:10).

Catholic and Orthodox tradition see Mary, the mother of Jesus, here, and the image shapes much Christian art: Mary standing on the moon crowned with stars. Our Lady of Guadalupe (Mexico, 1531) is pictured this way. The Catholic Church reads 11:19–12:10 on the Feast of the Assumption (August 15). Many Protestant scholars accept a secondary reference to Mary within the larger picture of Israel.

After the birth she is persecuted and protected (12:13–17), carried on eagle's wings into the wilderness as Israel was (Exodus 19:4), and fed there 1,260 days. "The rest of her children" are those who "hold to the testimony about Jesus" (12:17). The woman continues as the people of God after Christ's ascension.

The "ancient serpent" fights the woman and her offspring, echoing God's promise in Genesis 3:15: "I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers." Revelation 12 is that war.

Other traditions · Greece and Egypt a parallel, not Scripture · probably known to John’s readers
Leto, Isis and the hunted mother

In the Greek myth, the dragon Python pursued the pregnant goddess Leto; she escaped to an island and gave birth to Apollo, who later killed the dragon. Ephesus claimed the birth happened nearby. In Egypt, Isis hid in the marshes from Set to protect her son Horus. Revelation 12 tells the same kind of story about the true Son, perhaps on purpose. See "End-times stories from other traditions."

From history and scholarship

In 2017 a widely shared claim said a rare star alignment in the constellation Virgo on September 23 fulfilled 12:1–2 and signaled the end. Astronomers noted that similar alignments have happened before, and nothing unusual followed. John calls the woman "a sign" (sēmeion), a symbol, not a horoscope.

God is Israel's husband: "Your Maker is your husband, the LORD Almighty is his name" (Isaiah 54:5); "I will betroth you to me forever" (Hosea 2:19–20). Paul calls Christ and the church husband and wife (Ephesians 5:25–32) and says he promised the Corinthians "to one husband, to Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:2). Jesus told wedding parables (Matthew 22:1–14; 25:1–13) and called himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19–20).

After his suicide, rumors said he was not really dead and would return from the east with Parthian armies. At least three impostors claimed to be him (Tacitus, Histories 2.8; Suetonius, Nero 57). Jewish and Christian writings picked up the legend: the Sibylline Oracles describe a matricide king fleeing beyond the Euphrates and coming back (4.119–139; 5.361–370). The beast whose fatal wound was healed (13:3) and that "once was, now is not, and is about to come" (17:8) fits that legend.

If Nero is the sixth king, "one is" (17:10), the book was written before 68. Most scholars instead think John wrote under Domitian and used Nero as the pattern: a returning Nero, a new persecutor. The poet Juvenal called Domitian "a bald Nero."

The original Jezebel was the Phoenician queen of King Ahab who promoted Baal worship in Israel and persecuted the prophets (1 Kings 16:31; 18:4; 2 Kings 9:22). John gives the name to a real local teacher, the way we might call someone "a Judas."
Thyatira had many trade guilds (wool, dyers, bronze workers), whose banquets honored patron gods. Her teaching seems to have made room for Christians to join in.

Revelation never calls her a prostitute; it says she teaches and commits "sexual sin," and her followers "commit adultery" with her. The Old Testament already linked the name to prostitution: "the prostitution and sorceries of your mother Jezebel" (2 Kings 9:22), meaning Baal worship. See the chapter 2 page for the four ways this has been read.
Some manuscripts, including Codex Alexandrinus, read "your wife Jezebel," which would make her the wife of the church's leader. Most modern editions read "the woman."

sections.b: Two groups in the churches: those who "hold to the teaching of Balaam" (2:14) and the Nicolaitans (2:6, 15), probably the same group or close allies. Ephesus hated their practices; Pergamum tolerated them.

A famous foreign prophet hired by King Balak of Moab to curse Israel. God made him bless Israel instead, after his donkey saw the angel he could not (Numbers 22–24). But afterward he advised Moab to lure Israel into idol feasts and sexual sin at Baal of Peor (Numbers 25:1–2; 31:16). In the New Testament, he is the prophet who "loved the wages of wickedness" (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11).

From history and scholarship

Balaam was a real name known outside the Bible. In 1967 archaeologists at Deir Alla in Jordan found plaster wall writing from about 800 BC that begins, "The account of Balaam son of Beor, who was a seer of the gods." It is one of the oldest references outside the Bible to a person named in the Old Testament.

Irenaeus (about AD 180) says they followed Nicolaus, one of the seven deacons chosen in Jerusalem (Acts 6:5), and "lived lives of unrestrained indulgence" (Against Heresies 1.26.3). Clement of Alexandria defended Nicolaus himself and said his followers twisted his words (Miscellanies 2.20; 3.4). Their teaching seems to have been that Christians could eat at idol feasts and that what you did with your body did not matter.

"Nicolaus" in Greek means "conquers the people" (nikā + laos). Jewish tradition explained "Balaam" in Hebrew as "swallows the people" (bala' 'am; Talmud, Sanhedrin 105a). Many scholars think John saw the two names as the same idea in two languages.

A popular later reading, found for example in Watchman Nee, took "Nicolaitans" as "conquering the laity" and saw in them the rise of a clergy class ruling over ordinary believers. It is a creative sermon point, not what the Nicolaitans were in the first century.

"Synagogue" means "gathering." The Greek Old Testament calls Israel "the congregation (synagōgē) of the LORD" (Numbers 27:17; 31:16). John's phrase turns that around: a gathering that serves the accuser instead of the Lord. James uses "synagogue" even for a Christian assembly (James 2:2), so the word was not yet a label for "the other religion."

John is a Jewish writer, and the dispute is about who belongs to Israel's Messiah. "Satan" means "accuser," and these local opponents may have been accusing Christians before Roman officials. Smyrna's later bishop Polycarp was martyred around AD 155 after a crowd that included local Jews called for his death (Martyrdom of Polycarp 12–13). John's Gospel shows the same painful split (John 8:44; 9:22; 16:2).

The phrase has been used to justify hatred of Jews, from medieval sermons to modern hate groups. That reading turns a family argument in the first century into a weapon John never intended. Paul makes a similar point to John's in Romans 2:28–29, and in Romans 11 insists that God has not rejected his people.

sections.h: From a place to a person
sections.b: In the Old Testament, Abaddon is a place, the realm of the dead and destruction: "Death and Abaddon lie open before the LORD" (Proverbs 15:11; also Job 26:6; 28:22; Psalm 88:11). The Dead Sea Scrolls' Thanksgiving Hymns speak of "the torrents of Belial" bursting into Abaddon (1QH 11). Revelation turns the place into a ruler, the king of the locusts.

Readers disagree whether he is Satan himself, a chief demon, or a good angel carrying out God's judgment (since the locusts can only harm those without God's seal, 9:4). Proverbs 30:27 says "locusts have no king," which makes it striking that these do.

Apollyon sounds very like Apollo. The locust was one of Apollo's symbols; Athens had a statue of "Apollo the Locust-God" (Pausanias 1.24.8). Emperors liked to be linked with Apollo: Augustus built him a temple, and Nero performed as Apollo the singer. Many scholars think John is making a pointed joke: Rome's patron god is really the Destroyer, king of a demonic plague.
John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress (1678) has Christian fight Apollyon, a scaled monster with wings like a dragon, in the Valley of Humiliation.
The nations Satan gathers for the final battle after the thousand years, "as many as the sand on the seashore" (20:8). They surround "the city he loves" and are consumed by fire from heaven.

Magog is a grandson of Noah through Japheth (Genesis 10:2); Josephus identified his descendants with the Scythians of the far north (Antiquities 1.123). In Ezekiel 38–39, Gog is a ruler "of the land of Magog," leading northern nations against restored Israel, defeated by God with earthquake, fire and hail. Revelation makes both names into peoples "at the four corners of the earth": no longer one northern enemy but all the rebellious nations.

Over the centuries Gog and Magog have been identified with the Goths, Huns, Mongols, Turks and others. In the 20th century, the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) and later Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970) taught that "Rosh, Meshech and Tubal" (Ezekiel 38:2) meant Russia, Moscow and Tobolsk. Most scholars of Hebrew read rosh as "chief" ("chief prince of Meshech and Tubal") and locate Meshech and Tubal in ancient Anatolia.

The Qur'an tells of Dhul-Qarnayn, often identified with Alexander the Great, who built a wall of iron and copper to shut in Gog and Magog (Ya'juj and Ma'juj) until the end, when they will pour out (Qur'an 18:94–99; 21:96). Numbers 1 counts Israel's fighting men by tribe. The 144,000 "did not make themselves impure with women" (14:4), like soldiers keeping themselves pure before holy war (Deuteronomy 23:9–10; 1 Samuel 21:5). They are an army that wins by following the Lamb "wherever he goes" (14:4).

John "heard the number" (7:4) and then "looked, and there was a huge crowd that no one could count" (7:9). In 5:5–6 he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb. Many readers think the countable army and the countless crowd are the same people seen two ways: Israel's promised army, fulfilled in a multinational crowd.

claude.title: Dan is missing here, but first in line at the end
claude.body: Dan is left out of the sealing. But in Ezekiel's vision of restored Israel, Dan is the first tribe given land (Ezekiel 48:1) and has its own gate in the city (Ezekiel 48:32). Revelation 21 borrows Ezekiel's twelve-gated city and does not list which tribes. I suspect Dan's absence in chapter 7 marks judgment on idolatry (Judges 18:30; 1 Kings 12:29) for that period, not a final exclusion. The worst tribe still gets a gate.

sections.b: Rome had a punishment called relegatio ad insulam, "banishment to an island." It was used for people who were troublesome but not worth executing, often people of some standing. The wording of 1:9, "because of the word of God and my testimony," most naturally means John was sent there for preaching. A few scholars suggest instead that he went there to preach, but the phrase is used elsewhere in Revelation for suffering (6:9; 20:4), and John calls himself a "partner in suffering" in the same verse.

Irenaeus (about AD 180) says the vision was seen "toward the end of Domitian's reign" (Against Heresies 5.30.3), which would be about AD 95. Clement of Alexandria (about 200) says John "returned from the island after the tyrant died" and went back to Ephesus to appoint leaders in the churches. Eusebius (about 325) says the emperor Nerva freed people exiled by Domitian in AD 96 (Church History 3.18–20). Tertullian adds a legend that John was first plunged into boiling oil in Rome and survived. These traditions are early but not certain; see the page on dating.

John writes in the past tense ("I was on the island called Patmos"), and some scholars think he wrote the book after he had left. Others think he wrote it there. Either way, the vision came while he was cut off by sea from the seven churches he cared for, which may be part of why the book ends with "the sea was no more" (21:1).

The Monastery of Saint John the Theologian was founded in 1088 by the monk Christodoulos, with a grant from the Byzantine emperor Alexios I. Partway down the hill, the Cave of the Apocalypse is shown as the place where John received the vision; a split in the rock ceiling is said to be where the voice came through. Greek Orthodox Christians still keep a festival for John there every year.

Two churches get no rebuke (Smyrna and Philadelphia), and they are the two that are poor and pressured. Laodicea, the rich one, gets no praise.

There were other churches nearby: Colossae, Hierapolis, Troas, Miletus. Seven is Revelation's number of completeness, so seven churches can stand for the whole church. William Ramsay noticed that the seven sit on a circular road, each about 30 to 50 miles from the next, and that each was a center from which a letter could be copied and passed to smaller towns. A messenger landing at Ephesus would visit them in exactly the order of chapters 2–3.

Every letter has the same parts: (1) "To the angel of the church in... write," (2) a title of Jesus taken from the vision in chapter 1, (3) "I know what you do," (4) praise, rebuke, or both, (5) a call to repent or hold on, (6) "Whoever has ears should listen to what the Spirit says to the churches," and (7) a promise "to the one who wins the victory." The promises all point forward to chapters 21–22, where each is fulfilled.

The letters are full of references to each city's history and geography, which Colin Hemer catalogued in detail: Laodicea's lukewarm water and eye medicine, Sardis's acropolis captured by surprise, Philadelphia's earthquakes, Smyrna's "crown." See each city's page.

sections.h: A city of Artemis and the emperors
sections.b: The temple of Artemis was about four times the size of the Parthenon. Its silversmiths rioted when Paul's preaching hurt their trade, shouting "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" for two hours (Acts 19:23–41). Under Domitian, Ephesus also built a temple to the Flavian emperors with a colossal statue (its head and arm survive), and proudly took the title neokoros, "temple-keeper" of the emperor.

Paul spent over two years there (Acts 19:10) and warned its elders that "savage wolves" would come (Acts 20:29–30). The letter praises them for exactly that vigilance: they "tested those who call themselves apostles" (2:2). About fifteen years later, Ignatius of Antioch praised Ephesus for the same thing (To the Ephesians 9.1). Their problem was not false teaching but lost love (2:4).

Ephesus fought its river for centuries: the Cayster kept silting up the harbor, and the city had already been moved once. Today the ruins stand several miles from the sea. The church itself flourished for a long time. A great church council met there in 431, and Justinian built a huge basilica over the traditional tomb of John. But by the late Middle Ages the city was abandoned. Many readers see the threat of 2:5 in that history; the text, though, makes it conditional on repentance, not geography.

The promise of "the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God" (2:7) may contrast with Artemis's sanctuary, which, according to tradition, began as a tree shrine and offered asylum to fugitives. Jesus offers a better tree and a true refuge.

Smyrna built a temple to the goddess Roma in 195 BC, before Rome was even a great power in the east. In AD 26, eleven cities of Asia competed for the honor of building a temple to the emperor Tiberius; the Roman senate chose Smyrna (Tacitus, Annals 4.55–56). In such a city, refusing to honor the emperor was a public scandal.

sections.h: "Who died and came back to life"
sections.b: Old Smyrna was destroyed by the Lydians around 600 BC and lay in villages for about three centuries, until it was refounded on a new site after Alexander. The city had, in a sense, "died and lived again." Jesus introduces himself to them the same way (2:8).

The ring of public buildings on Mount Pagos above the city was called "the crown of Smyrna," and crowns (victors' wreaths) were common on its coins and in its festivals. Jesus promises a crown that lasts (2:10).

About sixty years after Revelation, Smyrna's bishop Polycarp, a man who had known John, was arrested and urged to say "Caesar is Lord" and offer incense. He answered, "Eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me?" He was burned in the stadium around AD 155 (Martyrdom of Polycarp 8–9). The account says local Jews joined the crowd against him, a sad echo of 2:9.
Of the seven cities, Smyrna is the only one that is still a great city today. It had a large Christian population until the burning of 1922.

Readers have pointed to four candidates. (1) The Great Altar of Zeus, a giant horseshoe-shaped structure on the hilltop, now rebuilt in Berlin's Pergamon Museum. (2) The temple of Rome and Augustus, the first in Asia, which made Pergamum a leader of emperor worship. (3) The sanctuary of Asclepius, the healing god, whose symbol was a snake and who was called "Savior." (4) The Roman court, since the governor held trials there. The most likely meaning is the city's role as a center of emperor worship and Roman power, where refusing it could cost your life (Antipas, 2:13).

The library at Pergamum was said to hold 200,000 scrolls; Plutarch reports that Mark Antony gave them to Cleopatra for the library of Alexandria. According to Pliny, when Egypt stopped exporting papyrus, Pergamum developed treated animal skins for writing. The word "parchment" comes from the city's name (pergamena).
Roman governors had the "right of the sword" (ius gladii), the power to execute. Jesus presents himself as the one who really "has the sharp two-edged sword" (2:12, 16).
"My faithful witness" (2:13) is the only Christian martyr named in Revelation. Later tradition says he was the city's bishop and was roasted to death in a bronze bull.

sections.h: Hidden manna and the white stone
sections.b: Jewish tradition said Jeremiah hid the ark, with the jar of manna, until the Messiah came (2 Maccabees 2:4–8; 2 Baruch 6:7–10; 29:8). White stones were used as votes for acquittal, as tickets to public banquets, and as amulets with secret names. Jesus offers all three: acquittal, a seat at his feast, and a name of his own giving (2:17).

More trade associations are named in Thyatira's inscriptions than in almost any other city of Asia. Lydia, Paul's first convert in Europe, was "a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira" (Acts 16:14). Guild membership meant guild banquets in honor of the gods, which is the setting of the "Jezebel" problem. See the chapter 2 page and the page on Jezebel.

The Greek chalkolibanon (2:18; 1:15) is a rare word found almost nowhere else. Colin Hemer argued it was a local alloy made by Thyatira's bronze workers. Coins of Thyatira show its god as a smith, and Jesus introduces himself as "the Son of God" (the only time in the book), perhaps answering the city's "son of Zeus," Apollo.

The promise (2:26–27) quotes Psalm 2, a coronation psalm. For working people in a small garrison town who could lose their livelihood by refusing guild feasts, Jesus promises them a share in his rule.

In the 300s, the writer Epiphanius reported that the church in Thyatira had been taken over by the Montanists, a prophetic movement from Phrygia, and that some critics of Revelation claimed there had never been a church there at all (Panarion 51.33). Akhisar today has almost nothing left of the ancient city.

Sardis sat on a high, steep acropolis that everyone thought could not be taken. Yet it fell twice by surprise because no one was watching. In 547 BC a Persian soldier saw a defender climb down a crack in the cliff to fetch a dropped helmet, and that night Cyrus's men climbed up the same way (Herodotus 1.84). In 214 BC Antiochus III's men did almost the same thing (Polybius 7.15–18). "If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour" (3:3).

The legendary wealth of Croesus came from gold washed down the Pactolus. In AD 17 a great earthquake struck twelve cities of Asia, and Sardis worst of all. Tiberius gave ten million sesterces and five years free of taxes (Tacitus, Annals 2.47). Sardis rebuilt and named itself in his honor.
Sardis was a center of wool dyeing. The few who "have not stained their clothes" will walk with Jesus "in white" (3:4), the color of victory and purity.

Archaeologists found at Sardis the largest ancient synagogue ever discovered, a remodeled public hall used as a synagogue from about the 200s or 300s AD, right in the city center. Jews were prominent and respected there. Interestingly, the letter to Sardis says nothing about Jewish opposition.

About eighty years after Revelation, Sardis's bishop Melito wrote a famous Easter sermon and traveled to Israel to learn which books belonged in the Old Testament, the earliest Christian list we have.

The earthquake of AD 17 hit Philadelphia hard, and aftershocks went on for years. Strabo, writing at the time, says the walls cracked daily and many people lived in the countryside, afraid to stay in the city (Geography 12.8.18; 13.4.10). Jesus promises, "I will make you a pillar in the temple of my God, and you will never leave it" (3:12): a building that will never shake, and no more running out of the city.

After the earthquake, the city took the name Neocaesarea ("New Caesar's city") to thank Tiberius, and later Flavia, honoring the emperor Vespasian's family. Its name kept changing with its patrons. Jesus promises names that last: "the name of my God, the name of the city of my God... and my own new name" (3:12).

Philadelphia was founded to spread Greek culture inland, a doorway to Phrygia. Jesus holds "the key of David" (Isaiah 22:22) and sets before the church "an open door that no one can shut" (Revelation 3:8): perhaps a door for mission, perhaps the door into the kingdom that the "synagogue of Satan" said was closed to them.

sections.h: "An open door that no one can shut"
sections.b: Philadelphia remained a Christian Greek city long after the rest of the region fell. It held out, surrounded, until 1390, the last Byzantine city in inner Asia Minor to fall to the Ottomans. Alaşehir still has the standing pillars of a large Byzantine church.

sections.b: Laodicea sat where major trade roads crossed and grew wealthy from banking and wool. When the earthquake of AD 60 destroyed it, the city rebuilt with its own money and did not ask Rome for help (Tacitus, Annals 14.27). The Roman statesman Cicero had cashed letters of credit there a century earlier. The church took on the city's self-image (3:17).

sections.h: Gold, white clothes and eye salve
sections.b: Jesus's advice (3:18) lists the city's three industries and turns each around. Its banks: "buy from me gold refined in the fire." Its famous black wool: "white clothes to wear." Its medical school, known for a "Phrygian powder" used for eyes: "salve to put on your eyes, so that you can see."

Laodicea had no good water of its own. It piped water in through a stone aqueduct from springs several miles away, and the pipes found at the site are thick with mineral deposits. Hierapolis's hot springs were used for healing; Colossae had cold, fresh water. Since a 1958 article by Rudwick and Green, most scholars have read "hot" and "cold" as both good: useful hot water and refreshing cold water. Lukewarm is useless, the kind of water you spit out (3:15–16). The older reading, that "cold" means openly hostile, makes the verse say Jesus would prefer an enemy to a lukewarm friend.

Paul mentions a letter to Laodicea that was to be swapped with the Colossians (Colossians 4:16). It has not survived; a later forgery called the "Epistle to the Laodiceans" circulated in the Middle Ages.

sections.h: "I stand at the door and knock"
sections.b: The best-known verse in the letters (3:20) is spoken to a church, not to unbelievers: Jesus is outside his own church, asking to come in and eat with whoever opens. Holman Hunt's painting The Light of the World (1853) shows the door with no handle on the outside.

"The great city that rules over the kings of the earth" (17:18), pictured as a prostitute riding the beast. Her fall is announced in 14:8 and 16:19 and mourned in chapter 18. The chapter 18 page has a full study with a map; this page summarizes.

The empire that destroyed Jerusalem and the first temple in 586 BC and carried Judah into exile. After that, "Babylon" became a byword for proud empire against God (Isaiah 47; Jeremiah 50–51; Daniel 4:30). The prophets' songs over Babylon's fall supply much of Revelation 18's wording.

Jewish and Christian writers after AD 70 called Rome "Babylon," because Rome too destroyed the temple (1 Peter 5:13; 4 Ezra 3:1–2; 2 Baruch 11:1; Sibylline Oracles 5.143, 159). Rome sat on seven hills (Revelation 17:9) and ruled kings (17:18).

Jerusalem, as the unfaithful bride (many preterists, citing 11:8 and 18:24). A rebuilt Babylon in Iraq (some futurists; Saddam Hussein rebuilt parts of it in the 1980s). Papal Rome (the Reformers). A global system of trade and false worship.
The cargo list (18:12–13) moves from gold and silk to cattle and chariots, and ends with "slaves, that is, human lives." Babylon falls because its wealth is built on people.

"Five have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come" (17:10). Counting emperors is famously hard: start with Julius or Augustus? Count the three short emperors of AD 69 or skip them? Different counts give different dates for the book. See the page on Rome for a table of the emperors.

common: For John's first readers, Rome; for later readers, any power that acts like Rome.
uncommon: A literal rebuilt city on the Euphrates.
Unfaithful Jerusalem.

claude.title: "Come out of her" is about loyalties, not a moving van
claude.body: "Come out of her, my people" (18:4) quotes Jeremiah 51:45, where Jews in Babylon were told to leave the city. But Revelation's readers lived all over Asia, not in Rome. The reasons given are moral: "so that you will not take part in her sins" (18:4). My reading: John is calling Christians to withdraw from Babylon's economy of idolatry and exploitation while living inside it, the way the Laodiceans were told to "buy" from Jesus instead of the banks (3:18). Many scholars read 18:4 this way; the link to the Laodicean letter's market language is my own.

sections.b: Rome was known everywhere as "the city of seven hills." A coin of Vespasian (AD 71) shows the goddess Roma, armed, seated on seven hills beside the Tiber, with the wolf and twins at her feet. Revelation 17 redraws that coin: a woman seated on seven heads, "seven hills" (17:9), drunk with the blood of God's people.

Starting from Augustus and skipping the three short reigns of 68–69 makes Vespasian the sixth ("one is") and Titus the seventh ("for a little while"), which would date the book to the 70s. Starting from Julius Caesar and counting all of them gives Nero or Galba. Many scholars think seven is symbolic and the list cannot be counted.

At first Christians were seen as a Jewish group. Claudius expelled Jews from Rome around AD 49 after riots "at the instigation of Chrestus," probably a dispute over Christ (Suetonius, Claudius 25.4). Nero blamed Christians for the great fire of AD 64 and had them burned as torches and torn by dogs (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). Under Domitian, there is good evidence of local pressure and some executions, though not an empire-wide campaign. About AD 112, Pliny, governor of a province near Asia, wrote to the emperor Trajan that he executed Christians who refused to offer incense to the emperor's image and curse Christ (Letters 10.96). That letter shows exactly the situation Revelation 13 describes.

Rome's propaganda spoke of the Pax Romana, the Roman peace, and of a golden age of trade. Revelation gives the other side: the red horse "takes peace from the earth" (6:4), and the merchants' wealth includes "human lives" (18:13). The Briton Calgacus, in a speech written by Tacitus, said of Rome: "They make a desert and call it peace" (Agricola 30).

sections.b: Two Jerusalems run through the book: the earthly "great city... where their Lord was also crucified" (11:8), and the new Jerusalem coming down from heaven (3:12; 21:2). Readers disagree about how much of the book is about the earthly city.

If John wrote in the 90s, Jerusalem had been in ruins for about twenty-five years. In AD 70, after a long siege, Titus's army burned the temple. Josephus, who was there, describes famine, fire and slaughter, and a huge number of dead (Jewish War 6.420). If John wrote in the late 60s, the siege was about to begin. That one question shapes the whole preterist reading.

sections.b: "The camp of God's people, the city he loves" (20:9) is surrounded by Gog and Magog at the end of the thousand years. Premillennialists read earthly Jerusalem, the capital of Christ's reign. Amillennialists read the church, as Hebrews speaks of "the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem" (Hebrews 12:22).

The temple's inner court is measured and protected, but the outer court and "the holy city" are trampled for 42 months (11:1–2), echoing Jesus's words, "Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" (Luke 21:24).
