sections.b: Ezekiel's closing vision is a new temple and city with twelve gates named for the tribes and the name "The LORD is there" (Ezekiel 40–48; 48:30–35). Isaiah promises foundations of sapphire and gates of jewels (Isaiah 54:11–12). Tobit 13:16–17 describes Jerusalem rebuilt "with sapphire and emerald" and streets "paved with ruby and stones of Ophir." Among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a text scholars call the New Jerusalem, which tours a giant city with measured gates and streets. John gathers all these hopes, then makes one major change: no temple (Revelation 21:22).

sections.h: A city, a bride and a temple
sections.b: The city is a bride (21:2, 9–10), a place (21:16), and a sanctuary (21:22). The three pictures belong together: the city is God's people, and it is where God lives with them. "God's home is now with people" (21:3).

"Its gates will never be shut" (21:25), and "the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it" (21:24), quoting Isaiah 60. The kings who earlier made war on the Lamb (19:19) now bring tribute. Some see this as a hint of wide salvation; others as the nations already redeemed.

common: A real future home of God's people, described in symbolic language.
uncommon: A literal cube 1,400 miles high.
The present church only, with no future city.

sections.b: "Then I looked, and there was the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with him were 144,000" (14:1). The scene answers chapter 13, where the dragon stands on the sand of the sea and the beasts rise.

Zion is the hill where God placed his king: "I have installed my king on Zion, my holy mountain" (Psalm 2:6), the same psalm Revelation quotes about the iron rod (Revelation 2:27; 12:5; 19:15). Joel promises, "On Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance... among the survivors whom the LORD calls" (Joel 2:32), which may explain the 144,000 standing there as a rescued remnant.

In Jewish writings close to John's time, the Messiah stands on Mount Zion and destroys the gathered nations (4 Ezra 13:35–36). Revelation 14 sets up the opposite picture to chapter 13: the dragon on the sand, the beast rising from the sea, and a crowd marked with its name; then the Lamb on the mountain with a crowd marked with his Father's name.

Hebrews says believers "have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem" (Hebrews 12:22). Revelation 14:2–3 has the song "from heaven" and "before the throne," which suggests the scene is in heaven. Others read a literal gathering in Jerusalem.

Megiddo sits where the coastal road crosses the Carmel ridge into the Jezreel Valley, the natural battlefield of the land. The Carmel ridge, where Elijah faced the prophets of Baal, begins just to the northwest, and Nazareth is about 10 miles north across the valley: Jesus grew up looking down on it. Jerusalem is about 55 miles to the south.

A fortress city guarding the pass where the great coastal road crosses into the Jezreel Valley. Whoever held it controlled the trade road between Egypt and Mesopotamia. Pharaoh Thutmose III's battle there (around 1457 BC) is the first battle in history recorded in detail. Deborah and Barak defeated the Canaanite kings "at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo" (Judges 5:19). King Josiah was killed there trying to stop Pharaoh Necho (2 Kings 23:29), and the mourning for him became proverbial (Zechariah 12:11). In 1918 the British general Allenby defeated the Ottoman army there and took the title "Viscount Allenby of Megiddo."

sections.h: The puzzle: there is no mountain
sections.b: Megiddo is a mound on a plain, not a mountain. Suggestions include: (1) the nearby Carmel ridge, where Elijah defeated Baal's prophets (1 Kings 18); (2) a play on har mo'ed, "mount of assembly," where the king of Babylon boasted he would set his throne (Isaiah 14:13); (3) a symbol combining Megiddo's history of battles with the Old Testament picture of nations gathered against God's mountain (Ezekiel 38–39; Joel 3; Zechariah 14). The "Hebrew" note may itself be a clue that the name is meant to be decoded, like the "number of a person" in 13:18.

sections.h: The battle that is never fought
sections.b: Revelation gathers the kings for "the battle" three times (16:14; 19:19; 20:8), but never describes fighting. In 19:19–21 the beast and false prophet are captured and the armies killed "by the sword that came out of the rider's mouth." The war is won by a word. The word "Armageddon" now means any huge, final catastrophe, a meaning the text does not quite support.

At the sixth trumpet, four angels "bound at the great river Euphrates" are released with an army of two hundred million cavalry (9:14–16). At the sixth bowl the river dries up "to prepare the way for the kings from the east" (16:12). Both times the river is a dam holding back invasion, and God lets it go.

The Parthians beyond the Euphrates were the one power Rome never conquered. Their mounted archers destroyed a Roman army at Carrhae in 53 BC and killed the general Crassus, and they defeated another army in AD 62. They were famous for shooting backward while riding away, which may be behind the horses whose "power is in their mouths and in their tails" (9:19). A popular rumor said Nero had not really died but had fled to the Parthians and would return with their armies (Sibylline Oracles 4.119–139).

Herodotus says Cyrus took Babylon by diverting the Euphrates and marching in along the riverbed (Histories 1.191). Isaiah and Jeremiah speak of God drying up Babylon's waters (Isaiah 44:27; Jeremiah 50:38; 51:36). Drying up water is also how God led Israel out (Exodus 14) and in (Joshua 3). In Revelation 16 the drying is a judgment that opens the road for Babylon's enemies.

sections.b: In recent years the Euphrates has dropped sharply because of dams and drought, and some prophecy teachers have linked this to 16:12. Most commentators caution that the text is drawing on the river's history and symbolism, not predicting water levels.
Abyssos means "bottomless." In Revelation it is the deep prison of evil: locusts come up from it, the beast rises from it, and the dragon is locked in it for a thousand years.

11:7The beast from the abyss kills the two witnesses
17:8The beast "is about to come up out of the abyss and go to destruction"
20:1–3An angel with the key binds the dragon and seals him in it

The Greek Old Testament uses abyssos about thirty times, mostly for the Hebrew tehom, the deep waters of creation: "darkness was over the surface of the deep" (Genesis 1:2). It was the place of chaos God tamed at creation and the depths of the earth (Psalm 71:20). So the "abyss" and the "sea" (13:1) are two ways of saying the same thing: the beast rises from chaos.

In 1 Enoch, fallen angels are bound in a deep place in the earth until judgment (1 Enoch 10:4–6; 18–21). 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 speak of angels held in chains in darkness. The demons in the Gerasene man "begged Jesus not to order them to go into the abyss" (Luke 8:31). Paul uses the word for the realm of the dead (Romans 10:7).
The abyss has a key, and it is always given by God (9:1; 20:1). Jesus himself holds "the keys of death and of Hades" (1:18). Evil comes out only when it is let out, and it goes back when it is sent.

Other traditions · Babylon and Greece a parallel, not Scripture · shared picture, no direct borrowing
Apsu and Tartarus

In Babylonian myth, Apsu was the freshwater deep below the earth, and its partner Tiamat the salt sea, whom Marduk killed to make the world. In Greek myth, Tartarus was a pit as far below Hades as the sky is above the earth, where Zeus locked the defeated Titans. 2 Peter 2:4 uses a form of the word "Tartarus" for where sinful angels are held. The Greek word abyssos is not related to "Apsu," but the picture of a deep prison for defeated rebels was widely shared.

sections.b: The Old Testament said Moses built the tabernacle after a pattern shown on the mountain (Exodus 25:40), and Hebrews explains that the earthly sanctuary was "a copy and shadow of what is in heaven" (Hebrews 8:5). John is shown the reality behind the copy.

In 11:1–2 John measures "the temple of God and the altar" but not the outer court. Readers take this as (1) the real temple before its destruction in AD 70 (preterist), (2) a future rebuilt "third temple" (futurist), or (3) the church, which Paul calls "God's temple" (1 Corinthians 3:16; 2 Corinthians 6:16), protected inwardly while trampled outwardly (many others).

In the new Jerusalem there is no temple, "because the Lord God the All-Powerful and the Lamb are its temple" (21:22). The temple was always a means to an end: God living among his people. When that happens fully, the building is no longer needed. Jesus had already said, "Destroy this temple, and I will raise it again in three days," speaking of his body (John 2:19–21).

From history and scholarship

Today some Jewish and Christian groups prepare for a "Third Temple" in Jerusalem, training priests and making temple vessels. The Temple Mount is also the site of the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque, so the issue is one of the most sensitive in the world.

sections.b: Thronos appears 47 times in Revelation, more than in all the rest of the New Testament together. The book's central question is whose throne is real.

sections.b: The center of chapter 4. Everything else is placed "around" it: a rainbow, twenty-four thrones, seven lamps, a sea of glass, four living creatures. John never describes the one who sits on it, only light and color: "like jasper and carnelian" (4:3). The picture draws on Isaiah 6, Ezekiel 1 and Daniel 7.
Satan's throne at Pergamum (2:13), the throne the dragon gives the beast (13:2), and the beast's throne darkened by the fifth bowl (16:10). Every other power in the book is a borrowed or fake throne.

David Aune showed that the heavenly throne room looks like Roman imperial ceremony turned upside down. People praised the emperor with shouts of "Worthy!" and hymns; the elders sing "You are worthy, our Lord and God" (4:11), the very title Domitian liked: "our lord and god." Client kings laid their crowns before the emperor; when the Armenian king Tiridates came to Rome he laid his crown before Nero's image (Tacitus, Annals 15.29). The elders "lay their crowns before the throne" (4:10) of the true Lord.

Jesus sits with his Father on his throne (3:21), and the Lamb stands "in the center of the throne" (5:6). By the end there is one throne, "the throne of God and of the Lamb" (22:1, 3). And Jesus promises the one who wins a place with him on it (3:21; 20:4).
The last throne in the book is the throne of judgment (20:11), so terrible that earth and sky flee from it. See the page on the great white throne.
"And the sea was no more" (21:1). Thalassa appears 26 times in Revelation, and it plays several roles, almost all of them dark.

The beast rises from the sea (13:1), as Daniel's four beasts did (Daniel 7:2–3). In the Old Testament the sea is the home of Leviathan, the twisting sea monster that God will kill (Isaiah 27:1), and a picture of the nations raging (Isaiah 17:12–13). God's power is shown by his control of the sea (Job 38:8–11; Psalm 89:9; Mark 4:39).

sections.b: Rome's wealth came by sea. In chapter 18 the captains and sailors stand far off and mourn as they watch Babylon burn (18:17–19).

Before God's throne is "something like a sea of glass, clear as crystal" (4:6). Later it is "mixed with fire," and the victors stand beside it singing the song of Moses (15:2–3), like Israel beside the Red Sea after Pharaoh's army drowned.
"The sea gave up the dead that were in it" (20:13). People feared death at sea most, since a drowned body had no grave.
John was on Patmos, cut off from his churches by the sea. Many preachers have noted that "no more sea" would have meant something personal to him: no more separation.

Other traditions · Canaan and Babylon a parallel, not Scripture · imagery the Bible deliberately reuses
Yam, the sea god

At Ugarit, the Canaanite god Baal fights Yam ("Sea") and the seven-headed serpent Litan (Leviathan). In Babylon, Marduk kills Tiamat, the salt sea, and makes the world from her body. Israel's poets borrowed the picture to say the true God rules the sea (Psalm 74:13–14). Revelation goes further: the sea is not just defeated but gone.

claude.title: "No more sea" means no more barrier
claude.body: Solomon's temple had a huge bronze basin called "the Sea," where priests washed before they served (1 Kings 7:23; 2 Chronicles 4:6). In Revelation 4 the sea of glass stands between the throne and everyone else. In the new creation there is no sea and no temple, and the people see God's face (22:4). My speculation: "no more sea" also means no more barrier and no more need for washing before you may come near, because the washing has already happened ("they washed their robes," 7:14; 22:14).

claude.title: Seven times "Lord God, the All-Powerful"?
claude.body: It is tempting to find sevens everywhere, so I checked one. The title pantokratōr, "the All-Powerful," appears 9 times (1:8; 4:8; 11:17; 15:3; 16:7, 14; 19:6, 15; 21:22), which does not fit the pattern. Not every repeated word is counted, and readers should be careful not to over-find patterns.

The same span is both the time of the enemy’s power and the time of God’s protection and witness.

Daniel 7:25 and 12:7 ("a time, times, and half a time"), and the half-"week" of Daniel 9:27. Elijah's drought, which Luke 4:25 and James 5:17 both say lasted three and a half years. And the Maccabean crisis, when Antiochus IV desecrated the temple from December 167 to December 164 BC, roughly the period Daniel describes.

Several events in John's century lasted about this long. Nero's persecution ran from the fire of AD 64 to his death in June 68, and the Jewish war from spring 67 to the fall of Jerusalem in August 70. Preterists point to these.

Using the day-for-a-year rule, historicists counted 1,260 years. Two favorite reckonings were AD 538 (when the bishop of Rome gained power over the Ostrogoths' city) to 1798 (when Napoleon's general took Pope Pius VI prisoner), and 606/607 to 1866/1867. Millerite and Adventist teaching built on such dates.

claude.title: It is Elijah’s number
claude.body: The Old Testament says Elijah's drought ended "in the third year" (1 Kings 18:1), yet both Jesus (Luke 4:25) and James (James 5:17) call it three and a half years. That means by the first century the drought was remembered as a 3½-year period. Revelation's two witnesses "shut the sky so that no rain falls during the days they are prophesying" (11:6), for 1,260 days. I think John chose the number partly because it was Elijah's: a time of prophetic witness in a hostile land, with God's people fed in the wilderness (12:6, like Elijah in 1 Kings 17:3–6). Others have noted the Elijah link; tying it to the woman's being "fed" is my addition.

About twenty different tribal lists appear in the Old Testament, and none matches Revelation’s.

Ten northern tribes were scattered by Assyria in 722 BC. In Jesus's day Jews still spoke of twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28; James 1:1; Acts 26:7), expecting God to gather them again (Ezekiel 37:15–28). Revelation pictures that gathering complete.

Dan and Ephraim were linked with idolatry: the tribe of Dan set up an idol (Judges 18:30), and King Jeroboam put golden calves at Bethel in Ephraim and at Dan (1 Kings 12:28–30). Irenaeus, about AD 180, said the Antichrist would come from Dan, citing Jeremiah 8:16 ("the snorting of his horses is heard from Dan") (Against Heresies 5.30.2). Others think the list simply needed exactly twelve once Levi and Joseph were added.

John "heard the number" of the sealed, 144,000 from the tribes (7:4), then "looked, and there was a huge crowd that no one could count, from every nation" (7:9). In chapter 5 he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb. Many readers think the second picture explains the first.
"The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches" (1:20). Jesus walks among the lampstands and holds the stars in his right hand.

The tabernacle had a single seven-branched gold lampstand, the menorah, which priests tended every evening and morning (Exodus 25:31–40; 27:20–21). Zechariah saw a lampstand fed by two olive trees, with the message "Not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit" (Zechariah 4:1–6). John sees seven separate lampstands: the light that once stood in one sanctuary is now spread among the churches of the world.

After Jerusalem fell, the temple's gold menorah was carried through Rome in Titus's victory parade in AD 71. The Arch of Titus, built by Domitian after Titus died in 81, still shows Roman soldiers carrying it. John's readers knew where Israel's lampstand had gone. In Revelation, the risen Jesus walks among lampstands Rome cannot carry off.

Ephesus is warned, "I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you turn back" (2:5). A church can stop being a church. The two witnesses are also called "the two olive trees and the two lampstands" (11:4).

Ancient people saw stars as heavenly beings (Job 38:7; Judges 5:20). A coin of Domitian's wife shows their dead infant son as a new god, seated on the globe of the world with seven stars around him. Jesus holding seven stars claims the place the emperors' propaganda gave to their own family.

Several kinds of document had this shape. Roman wills were sealed by seven witnesses and could be opened only after the death of the one who made them. Deeds and contracts were written on the inside and summarized on the outside (compare Jeremiah 32:10–14). Ezekiel's scroll was written "on the front and back" with laments (Ezekiel 2:9–10). Ezekiel names God's "four dreadful judgments: sword and famine and wild beasts and plague" (Ezekiel 14:21), the same four as 6:8. sections.b: Irenaeus and many others took him as Christ or the gospel going out, since Christ rides a white horse in 19:11. Others note that this rider has a bow, not a sword from his mouth, and that the next three riders are all disasters; they see a false conqueror or simply military conquest. Rome's feared enemies, the Parthians, were mounted archers known for white horses.

"A quart of wheat for a denarius" (6:6) was about eight to sixteen times the normal price; a laborer's whole day's pay would buy food for one person. "Do not harm the oil and the wine" may reflect a real event: in AD 92 Domitian ordered half the vineyards in the provinces cut down to grow more grain, then backed down after protests from Asia (Suetonius, Domitian 7.2; 14.2).
"Pale" is chlōros, the green-gray color of a corpse (our word "chlorine" comes from it). Death rides it, and Hades, the grave, follows like a wagon picking up bodies.
Albrecht Dürer's 1498 woodcut made the four riders the most famous image in Revelation, and they have appeared in films, novels and music ever since.
Seven angels blow seven trumpets (8:2–11:19). The first four strike nature, the next two strike people, and the last three are called "woes." Many of them repeat the plagues of Egypt.

sections.b: Israel's ram's-horn and silver trumpets called the people to battle and to festivals, announced a new king, and warned of attack. At Jericho, seven priests blew seven trumpets for seven days, and the walls fell (Joshua 6). The prophets spoke of "the day of the trumpet and battle cry" (Zephaniah 1:16), and Paul of "the last trumpet" at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:52). Leviticus 23:24 sets a festival of trumpets.

The trumpets hit "a third," never everything. Their purpose is to call people to repent, but "the rest of humanity... did not repent" (9:20–21). This is why the seventh trumpet is followed by worship, not destruction.

Between the sixth and seventh trumpets comes a long interlude: the mighty angel and the little scroll (10:1–11) and the two witnesses (11:1–14). The same thing happens between the sixth and seventh seals (chapter 7).

The two series follow the same order, and both echo the plagues of Egypt. Many scholars think they describe the same judgments from two angles, with growing intensity, not two different events.

The gold bowls first appear in 5:8, "full of incense, which are the prayers of God's people." The bowls of wrath are handed out from the heavenly temple. Many readers connect them: the prayers of the martyrs, "How long, Sovereign Lord, until you judge?" (6:10), are answered in the bowls. The third bowl's angel says, "They poured out the blood of your holy people... and you have given them blood to drink" (16:6).
Three times the people "cursed the name of God" and "did not repent" (16:9, 11, 21). The bowls show that judgment alone does not change hearts.

Right in the middle of the sixth bowl comes a blessing: "Look, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake" (16:15). Even here, the book speaks to its readers, not just about the world.

In the ancient world, a seal pressed into wax or clay showed ownership, protected a document from tampering, and marked it as genuine. Slaves and soldiers were sometimes tattooed or branded with their owner's or general's mark. A seal on the forehead says, "This person belongs to God, and is under his protection."

Ezekiel saw a man with a writing kit put a mark on the foreheads of those who grieved over Jerusalem's sins; the executioners were told to spare them (Ezekiel 9:4–6). The mark was the Hebrew letter tav, which in the old script was written like an X or a cross. Early Christians noticed.
The blood on Israel's doorposts was a sign so that "the destroyer" would pass over (Exodus 12:13, 23). The sealed in Revelation are likewise protected from the plagues (9:4).
The locusts cannot harm those with the seal (9:4). But sealed people still die as martyrs (6:9–11; 13:7). The seal protects from God's wrath and from losing faith, not from the world's hatred.

sections.h: The seal in the early church
sections.b: Paul says believers have been "sealed with the promised Holy Spirit" (Ephesians 1:13; 4:30; 2 Corinthians 1:22). By the second century, Christians called baptism "the seal" (2 Clement 7:6; Shepherd of Hermas, Similitudes 9.16).

From history and scholarship

A striking parallel: according to 3 Maccabees 2:29, the Egyptian king Ptolemy IV ordered Jews to be branded with the ivy leaf of Dionysus, the sign of his god, before they could enjoy civic rights. Being marked for a god in order to take part in public life was not an unknown idea.
Promised to Ephesus (2:7) and standing on both banks of the river in the city (22:2), "producing twelve kinds of fruit," with leaves "for healing the nations." It is the Bible's last picture of Eden.

God placed the tree of life in the middle of the garden (Genesis 2:9). After Adam and Eve sinned, God guarded "the way to the tree of life" with cherubim and a flaming sword (Genesis 3:22–24). Ezekiel saw a river from the temple lined with trees bearing fruit every month, whose leaves heal (Ezekiel 47:12). Revelation brings both together.

Proverbs calls wisdom "a tree of life to those who take hold of her" (Proverbs 3:18). In 1 Enoch 24–25, a fragrant tree near God's throne will be given to the righteous after the judgment. The Testament of Levi says the Messiah "will open the gates of paradise" and give the saints to eat from the tree of life (18:10–11).

Revelation's word for tree is xylon, which also means "wood." The apostles use the same word for the cross: "whom they killed by hanging him on a tree" (Acts 5:30; 1 Peter 2:24). Early Christian writers and artists loved this connection: the cross is the tree of life.

The KJV says "book of life," but the Greek manuscripts say "tree of life." Erasmus had no Greek manuscript of the last verses and translated them back from Latin, where a copying error had changed "tree" (ligno) to "book" (libro).

Other traditions · Ancient Near East a parallel, not Scripture · shared hope, different meaning
Sacred trees

Assyrian palace carvings show winged spirits tending a stylized "sacred tree," and many cultures told of a world tree or a tree of immortality (the Norse Yggdrasil; the plant of youth in the Epic of Gilgamesh, stolen by a snake). The Ephesian sanctuary of Artemis was also said to have begun at a sacred tree. Genesis and Revelation share the hope of a tree that gives life, but tie it to the one God.

claude.title: Eden’s guard becomes twelve angels at open gates
claude.body: After the fall, God placed cherubim at Eden "to guard the way to the tree of life" (Genesis 3:24). In the new Jerusalem there are angels at the gates again, twelve of them (21:12), but the gates are never shut (21:25), and 22:14 blesses those who "go through the gates" to the tree of life. My speculation: the angels at the gates are Eden's guard turned around, standing beside open doors instead of blocking the way.

sections.b: "God's temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant could be seen in his temple" (11:19). The most famous lost object in history appears for one verse.

The Bible never says. Theories include: Pharaoh Shishak took it (1 Kings 14:25–26); Babylon took or destroyed it in 586 BC; Jeremiah hid it in a cave on Mount Nebo until God gathers his people (2 Maccabees 2:4–8); an angel hid it in the earth until the end (2 Baruch 6:7–10); or it was taken to Ethiopia, where the Ethiopian Orthodox Church says it is kept at Aksum. Jeremiah himself said a day would come when "they will no longer say, ‘The ark of the covenant of the LORD’... it will not be missed" (Jeremiah 3:16).

The ark was the throne of God's presence and the place of atonement. After the seventh trumpet, the hidden presence of God is opened to view, with lightning, thunder and earthquake as at Sinai. Its appearance says God has not forgotten his covenant.

Jewish tradition said the jar of manna was hidden with the ark and would come back in the days of the Messiah (2 Baruch 29:8). Jesus's promise of "hidden manna" to Pergamum (2:17) probably draws on that hope.

The ark appears in 11:19 and the woman "clothed with the sun" in 12:1, with no break in the original. Some Catholic and Orthodox readers link the two and call Mary the "ark of the new covenant," since she carried the Word in her womb (compare Luke 1:35, 39–56 with 2 Samuel 6:2–16). Most Protestant readers see the woman as God's people.

sections.b: Ezekiel was handed a scroll "written on the front and back," told to eat it, and found it "as sweet as honey" before he was sent to a rebellious people (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3). Jeremiah said, "When your words came, I ate them; they were my joy" (Jeremiah 15:16). Eating the scroll means taking God's message completely inside.

The word of God is sweet to receive, and bitter to carry, because it contains judgment and suffering, for the world and for the messenger. Chapter 11, which follows immediately, is the story of witnesses who prophesy and are killed.

sections.h: Little scroll or the same scroll?
sections.b: John uses a diminutive word, biblaridion, "little scroll." Many think it holds chapter 11 or chapters 11–22. Richard Bauckham argues that it is the same as the sealed scroll of chapter 5, now opened, and that its message is the story of the witnessing church that follows. It is "little" only next to the giant angel.
The angel stands on sea and land and swears by the Creator that "there will be no more delay" (10:6), echoing the angel in Daniel 12:7 who swore it would be "a time, times, and half a time."

Psalm 29 calls God's voice thunder seven times: "The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders." When God spoke to Jesus, the crowd "said it had thundered" (John 12:28–29). The seven thunders are a full message from God.

Thunder marks God speaking and each seventh judgment, growing louder each time (8:5; 11:19; 16:18). The only thunder John may not write down is the one in chapter 10.

Several readings: (1) It was a further cycle of judgments that God canceled, choosing "no more delay" and the call to witness instead (Richard Bauckham). (2) It is a reminder that not everything is revealed: "The secret things belong to the LORD our God" (Deuteronomy 29:29). Paul too heard "things that cannot be told" (2 Corinthians 12:4). (3) It was meant for John alone.

Through the centuries some have claimed to reveal what the thunders said. In the 1960s the American evangelist William Branham taught that their meaning was being revealed in his ministry. Most churches have warned that the text itself tells us not to fill this gap.

Ancient "sapphire" was usually lapis lazuli, and ancient "topaz" was usually peridot, from an island in the Red Sea.

Exodus 28:17–21 lists twelve stones set in four rows on the high priest's breastplate, each engraved with the name of a tribe. Eight of Revelation's twelve match the Greek Old Testament's list. In the new Jerusalem, the names of the tribes are on the gates and the names of the apostles on the jeweled foundations (21:12–14): the whole city is dressed like a high priest.

"I will build your foundations with lapis lazuli. I will make your battlements of rubies, your gates of sparkling jewels" (Isaiah 54:11–12). Tobit 13:16–17 pictures Jerusalem's walls of precious stones. Babylon wears jewels as decoration (17:4); the city of God is built of them.

The first-century writers Philo and Josephus linked the breastplate's twelve stones with the twelve signs of the zodiac. R. H. Charles noticed that Revelation's order is close to a traditional order of zodiac stones reversed, as if the city undoes the claims of astrology. Others doubt the pattern, since the ancient lists vary.

Wormwood (Artemisia absinthium) is a bitter herb, used in ancient medicine against intestinal worms (hence its name) and later to flavor absinthe. It is named after the goddess Artemis, the great goddess of Ephesus. It is bitter but not usually deadly.

Wormwood is the Old Testament's taste of judgment and of sin. "I will feed this people wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink" (Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15). "You who turn justice into wormwood" (Amos 5:7). Moses warned against "a root that produces poison and wormwood," a person who turns away to other gods (Deuteronomy 29:18). Lamentations 3:15, 19 uses it for the bitterness of exile.

sections.b: Stars falling from the sky are signs of judgment (Isaiah 34:4; Mark 13:25), and in Revelation stars can be angels or rulers (1:20; 9:1). Isaiah calls the fallen king of Babylon "morning star, son of the dawn" (Isaiah 14:12).

The Ukrainian word chornobyl names mugwort (Artemisia vulgaris), a close relative of wormwood. After the 1986 nuclear disaster, which poisoned the water and land of a huge area, many people connected the two, and some Ukrainian Orthodox writers spoke of it. Most commentators treat the link as a striking coincidence, not a fulfillment.

"Something like a sea of glass, clear as crystal" before the throne (4:6). Later it is "mixed with fire," and those who won the victory over the beast stand beside it with harps and sing the song of Moses (15:2–3).

Under God's feet at Sinai was "something like a pavement made of lapis lazuli, as clear as the sky itself" (Exodus 24:10). Over the living creatures in Ezekiel's vision was "an expanse, sparkling like ice" (Ezekiel 1:22). In 1 Enoch 14:9–10, the heavenly house is built of crystal with a floor of crystal. Solomon's temple had a great bronze basin called "the Sea" (1 Kings 7:23).

In chapter 15, the victors stand beside a sea "mixed with fire" and sing "the song of God's servant Moses and the song of the Lamb" (15:3). The picture is Israel on the far shore of the Red Sea, singing after Pharaoh's army drowned (Exodus 15). The sea that once threatened God's people has become the floor they stand on.

Glassblowing was invented in Syria and Palestine in the first century BC, and by John's day glass was common across the empire. Clear, colorless glass was harder to make and prized. "Glass clear as crystal" was a picture of perfect purity.

Other traditions · Jewish and Islamic tradition a parallel, not Scripture · shared picture
Floors that look like water

The Talmud tells of four rabbis who entered the "garden" of heavenly vision. Rabbi Akiva warned them, "When you reach the stones of pure marble, do not say, ‘Water, water’" (Hagigah 14b). The Qur'an tells how the Queen of Sheba, entering Solomon's palace, thought its floor was a pool of water and lifted her skirts, but it was "a palace paved smooth with glass" (Qur'an 27:44). In all three traditions, a sea of glass is the threshold of a holy king's presence.

A grain harvest by "one like a son of man" with a sharp sickle (14:14–16), and a grape harvest thrown into "the great winepress of God's anger" (14:17–20), whose blood flows 1,600 stadia.

Many readers see the grain harvest as the gathering of God's people, since Jesus used harvest for gathering believers (Matthew 13:30; Mark 4:29; John 4:35), and the reaper is "one like a son of man" (1:13). The grape harvest, cut by an angel from the altar, is judgment. Others read both as judgment, following Joel 3:13, which has both pictures in one verse: "Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. Come, trample the grapes, for the winepress is full."

Grapes were trampled by foot in a stone basin, and the juice ran out through a channel. Treading grapes was a common picture for judgment: "I have trodden the winepress alone... their blood spattered my garments" (Isaiah 63:1–6). Revelation 19:13–15 picks this up for the returning Christ.

The winepress was trodden "outside the city" (14:20). Hebrews says Jesus "suffered outside the city gate" (Hebrews 13:12). Some readers see a hint that the judgment falls where Jesus already suffered.

About 184 miles. 1,600 is 4 × 4 × 100, or 40 × 40, suggesting the whole world. Jerome noted that the land of Israel was about 160 Roman miles long, close to the same figure. "As high as horses' bridles" is a picture of overwhelming slaughter found also in 1 Enoch 100:3.

Julia Ward Howe's "Battle Hymn of the Republic" (1861) begins, "He is trampling out the vintage where the grapes of wrath are stored," drawing on this chapter and Isaiah 63. John Steinbeck took the title of his 1939 novel from it.

Daniel is told to "seal the book until the time of the end" (Daniel 12:4, 9). John is told the opposite: "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, because the time is near" (Revelation 22:10). Revelation presents itself as Daniel opened.

Daniel sees four beasts; John sees one beast made of all four, in reverse order, as if Rome sums up every empire. Daniel's "son of man" comes to the Ancient of Days; in Revelation, the son of man has the Ancient of Days' white hair (1:14), so Jesus shares God's identity. Daniel's saints receive the kingdom; in Revelation they reign because the Lamb has made them a kingdom (1:6; 5:10).

Traditionally, Daniel was written in the 500s BC by Daniel in Babylon. Many modern scholars date its visions to the 160s BC, during Antiochus IV's persecution. Either way, by John's time Daniel was read as a prophecy about the last empire and the coming kingdom, and Jewish writers such as 4 Ezra 12:11–12 openly reinterpreted Daniel's fourth beast as Rome.

By the last chapter, Jesus claims all three titles together (22:13).

Isaiah 44:6: "I am the first and I am the last; apart from me there is no God" (also Isaiah 41:4; 48:12). Jewish teachers pointed out that the Hebrew word for truth, emet, uses the first, middle and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and called it "the seal of God."

Revelation gives God's own titles to Jesus, one of the New Testament's strongest statements that Jesus shares God's identity. The same God who "is, and who was, and who is to come" (1:8) is the Jesus who says "I am coming soon" (22:12–13).
From the 300s on, Christians painted and carved the letters A and Ω beside the cross or the Chi-Rho monogram, on tombs, coins and church walls. They are still used on Easter candles.

Other traditions · Greece a parallel, not Scripture · a parallel John’s readers may have known
"Zeus was, Zeus is, Zeus will be"

The Greek traveler Pausanias records a chant of the priestesses at Dodona: "Zeus was, Zeus is, Zeus will be" (Description of Greece 10.12.10). Revelation's "who is, and who was, and who is to come" (1:4, 8) sounds similar, but notice the change: God is not "who will be" but "who is coming." He does not merely exist in the future; he arrives.

From history and scholarship

A popular modern teaching says the untranslated Hebrew word et (aleph-tav, the first and last letters) in Genesis 1:1 is a hidden name of Jesus. Hebrew grammarians point out that et is an ordinary grammar marker used thousands of times. The real Alpha-and-Omega background is Isaiah.

The words can be divided two ways: marana tha, "Our Lord, come!" (a prayer), or maran atha, "Our Lord has come" (a confession). Revelation 22:20 and Didache 10:6 show that the church understood it as a prayer.

Paul leaves it untranslated in a letter to Greek-speaking Corinthians (1 Corinthians 16:22), so it must have come from the very first Aramaic-speaking believers in Jerusalem and been used in worship everywhere. That matters: Aramaic-speaking Jews, within a few years of the resurrection, were already praying to Jesus as "Lord" (mar).

The Didache, a church manual from about John's time, ends its communion prayer: "Let grace come and let this world pass away. Hosanna to the God of David. If anyone is holy, let him come; if anyone is not, let him repent. Maranatha. Amen" (Didache 10:6). Revelation ends the same way: an invitation ("let anyone who is thirsty come," 22:17), a warning, and "Come, Lord Jesus."

The KJV prints 1 Corinthians 16:22 as "let him be Anathema Maranatha," and for centuries some readers took "Anathema Maranatha" as a single, extra-strong curse. In fact, "anathema" ends one sentence ("let him be cursed") and "Maranatha" is a separate prayer.

It opens and closes many psalms (Psalms 104–106, 111–113, 146–150). Psalms 113–118, called the Hallel, were sung at Passover; Jesus and his disciples sang them after the Last Supper (Mark 14:26).

sections.h: Praise at the fall of the wicked
sections.b: The rabbis noticed that the first "Hallelujah" in the book of Psalms comes at the end of Psalm 104, right after "May sinners vanish from the earth" (Psalm 104:35). The Talmud says David did not say Hallelujah until he saw the downfall of the wicked (Berakhot 9b–10a). Revelation's first Hallelujahs are also for the fall of Babylon. The praise is not gloating; it is relief that injustice is over.

The book of Tobit, written before Revelation, imagines the new Jerusalem built of jewels and says "all her lanes will cry Hallelujah" (Tobit 13:17–18). Revelation's hallelujahs come right before the bride and the new city.
Handel's "Hallelujah" chorus (1741) sets 19:6, 11:15 and 19:16: "For the Lord God omnipotent reigneth... King of Kings, and Lord of Lords."

The rider on the white horse is named "the Word of God" (19:13), the same title the Gospel of John gives Jesus (John 1:1, 14). In Revelation, God's word is both the message believers die for and the weapon Christ wins with.

Jesus's only weapon is a sword from his mouth (1:16; 2:16; 19:15, 21), from Isaiah 11:4, "With the breath of his lips he will slay the wicked," and Isaiah 49:2, "He made my mouth like a sharp sword." Hebrews says "the word of God is alive and active, sharper than any double-edged sword" (Hebrews 4:12). Revelation's final battle is won by speech.

sections.b: The closest parallel is in the Wisdom of Solomon, written before Revelation, describing the night of the Passover: "Your all-powerful word leaped from heaven, from the royal throne, into the midst of the land doomed to destruction, a stern warrior carrying the sharp sword of your authentic command" (Wisdom 18:15–16). Revelation 19 takes that picture and gives it a name.

sections.h: "The word of God and the testimony of Jesus"
sections.b: This pair runs through the book like a refrain: John writes it (1:2), is exiled for it (1:9), the martyrs die for it (6:9; 20:4), and the woman's children keep it (12:17). "Word of God" is what God has said; "testimony of Jesus" is the witness Jesus gave and his people continue.
"These words are trustworthy and true" (21:5; 22:6). The book ends by warning against adding to or taking away from its words (22:18–19), as Moses warned about the law (Deuteronomy 4:2).

sections.b: Across the ancient Near East a god defeats a sea dragon: Marduk splits Tiamat (Enuma Elish); Baal crushes Yam and Litan, "the mighty one with seven heads" (Ugarit, about 1300 BC). The Old Testament uses this picture for the true God (Psalm 74:13–14; Isaiah 27:1; 51:9). Revelation completes it.

In the Greek story, the dragon Python hunts the pregnant Leto; she escapes and gives birth to Apollo, who later kills the dragon. Ephesus claimed Leto gave birth near the city (Tacitus, Annals 3.61). Many scholars think Revelation 12 deliberately retells it with Jesus as the true child.

Zoroastrian teaching expects a final savior (the Saoshyant), resurrection, a river of molten metal that purifies, and the world "made wonderful" (Frashokereti). The dragon Azi Dahaka is chained in a mountain until the end, breaks free, and is destroyed: almost the shape of Revelation 20. Dating the Persian texts is difficult, so scholars debate who influenced whom.

Fimbulwinter (war and hunger before the end), the wolf Fenrir bound until Ragnarök, fire, and a green world rising from the sea. These were written down by Christians around 1200, so borrowing may run either way.

claude.title: Revelation answers the stories its readers knew
claude.body: A similar image does not mean John borrowed his faith. Often he takes the most famous story in his readers' world and turns it around: the dragon-slaying god is Jesus, not Apollo; the seven-headed monster is not a cosmic rival but a creature that gets captured; the "goddess Roma" on seven hills is a drunk prostitute. Revelation is as much counter-myth as myth.

sections.b: This is the only time Revelation uses the noun "gospel" (euangelion). It is proclaimed "to every nation, tribe, language, and people" (14:6), and its content is a call to worship the Creator. "Fear God and give him glory" is the language of repentance: in 11:13, the survivors of the earthquake "were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven." It is a last invitation, not only a threat.

In the 1200s, the followers of Joachim of Fiore taught that a new age of the Spirit was dawning, and one Franciscan published an "Introduction to the Eternal Gospel" (1254) claiming Joachim's writings would replace the New Testament. The church condemned it.

Seventh-day Adventists see their own movement in these three messages, read in a historicist way: the first angel's "the hour of his judgment has come" fulfilled in the Millerite preaching of the 1840s, the second in the call to leave fallen churches, and the third as a warning linked to the Sabbath commandment. Most other traditions read them as a summary of the choice the whole book puts before every reader.
An odd, ominous phrase found only in Revelation (2:11; 20:6; 20:14; 21:8), defined as "the lake of fire."

The Aramaic Targums, the synagogue paraphrases of Scripture, use "the second death" for final judgment: "Let Reuben live, and not die the second death" (Targum Onkelos on Deuteronomy 33:6). The Targum of Jeremiah 51:39, 57 uses it of Babylon's rulers, who "will not live in the world to come."

Its first use is a promise to the suffering church in Smyrna: "The one who wins the victory will not be harmed by the second death" (2:11). Rome can cause the first death, not the second (Matthew 10:28).

"The second death has no power over" those who share in the first resurrection (20:6). Augustine: a first resurrection of the soul now and of the body later; a first death of the body and a second, final death. "Born once, die twice; born twice, die once."

sections.b: Pergamum (2:14) and Thyatira (2:20–21) pair it with eating food sacrificed to idols, as in Numbers 25:1–2 and Acts 15:29. Scholars debate how literal it is there; the chapter 2 page lays out the views.
The faithful are pictured as a bride (19:7–8; 21:2) and as those who "did not defile themselves" (14:4). The book moves from a prostitute city to a bride city.

common: In the letters it means mainly compromise with idolatry, with literal sin possibly included.
uncommon: It is entirely literal: a libertine group that taught sexual freedom.
The sexual language is mostly stock polemic against a rival teacher.

sections.b: The wording is almost a formula. Ephesus: "those who say they are apostles and are not" (tous legontas heautous apostolous kai ouk eisin). Smyrna: "those who say they are Jews and are not" (tōn legontōn Ioudaious einai heautous kai ouk eisin). Philadelphia repeats it and adds "but are lying" (alla pseudontai). Thyatira: "who calls herself a prophet" (hē legousa heautēn prophētin). Laodicea: "you say, I am rich" (legeis hoti plousios eimi). Each time the word "say" (legō) stands against what Jesus, who "knows" (2:2, 9, 19; 3:8, 15), says is true. Three of the claims are titles of honor in God's people: apostle, Jew, prophet. The fourth is a title of honor in the city: rich.

sections.h: It is John’s way of talking
sections.b: The same "say... but" formula runs through 1 John, which comes from the same circle of churches in Asia: "If we say we have fellowship with him and walk in darkness, we lie" (1 John 1:6). "Whoever says ‘I know him’ but does not keep his commandments is a liar" (1 John 2:4). "If anyone says ‘I love God’ and hates his brother, he is a liar" (1 John 4:20). In John's Gospel, Jesus tells opponents who say "Abraham is our father" that if they were Abraham's children they would act like it, and calls the devil "a liar and the father of lies" (John 8:39–44), the same pairing as "synagogue of Satan... they are lying" (Revelation 3:9). In this way of thinking, a name is a claim that your life either backs up or exposes.

sections.h: Apostles and prophets: testing the travelers
sections.b: Early churches were visited by traveling teachers who claimed to be apostles ("sent ones") or prophets. Churches had to test them. Paul warns of "false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:13), and 1 John says "test the spirits, because many false prophets have gone out" (1 John 4:1). A church manual from about the same time, the Didache, gives practical tests: a traveling apostle may stay one or two days, but "if he stays three days, he is a false prophet," and if he asks for money, he is a false prophet (Didache 11.5–6). "Not everyone who speaks in the Spirit is a prophet, but only if he has the ways of the Lord" (11.8). About fifteen years after Revelation, Ignatius of Antioch praised the Ephesians because some had come through "with evil teaching, whom you did not allow to sow among you" (To the Ephesians 9.1). Ephesus kept its reputation for testing.

sections.h: "Jew": an honored name and a legal status
sections.b: In the first century "Jew" (Ioudaios, from Judah) was more than a religion. It was a people, a way of life, and a legal category. Jews in the empire had long-standing rights: they could keep the Sabbath, send money to the temple, and were not required to sacrifice to the gods or the emperor. After AD 70 every Jew paid a special tax to Rome, the fiscus Judaicus, and the historian Suetonius says the emperor Domitian, in John's lifetime, prosecuted people "who lived as Jews without admitting it" or hid their origin (Domitian 12.2). So who counted as a Jew was decided in tax offices and courts, not only in synagogues. As followers of Jesus were pushed out of synagogues (John 9:22; 16:2), they lost that legal shelter and became visible to the authorities as members of an unlicensed new group. The "slander" (blasphēmia) at Smyrna may have been exactly that: telling officials, "These people are not Jews."

sections.h: Citizenship: a claim with life-and-death weight
sections.b: Claiming a status you did not have was a serious matter in the Roman world. Roman citizenship brought rights: a trial, an appeal to Caesar, freedom from flogging and crucifixion. So false claims were punished hard. Suetonius reports that the emperor Claudius had men who falsely claimed Roman citizenship beheaded (Claudius 25.3). In Acts, a Roman commander about to flog Paul is alarmed to learn he is a citizen; the commander bought his own citizenship, but Paul was "born a citizen" (Acts 22:25–29; compare Acts 16:37–38). The Stoic teacher Epictetus, who taught in Greece in John's day, even uses the same kind of phrase about Jewish identity: "Why do you act the part of a Jew when you are a Greek?... We are counterfeit, Jews in name but something else in fact" (Discourses 2.9.20–21). In that world, "they say they are... and are not" sounded like an accusation of fraud. Revelation answers with a better citizenship. Paul told the Roman colony of Philippi, "our citizenship is in heaven" (Philippians 3:20). Revelation ends with a city whose citizens are registered "in the Lamb's book of life" (21:27), and promises the faithful at Philadelphia that Jesus will write on them "the name of the city of my God" (3:12). The true citizen does not claim the name. He receives it.

sections.h: Who were "those who say they are Jews"?
sections.b: Scholars give four main answers. (1) Members of the local synagogues who opposed and reported the Christians. This is the most common view. John, himself a Jew, is saying that people who side with Rome against Israel's Messiah are not living up to the name, much as Paul says "a person is not a Jew who is one only outwardly" (Romans 2:28–29). (2) Gentiles who were adopting Jewish identity, perhaps to gain the legal protection, and who pressured Christians to do the same. David Frankfurter argues this, and Ignatius warned the Philadelphians a few years later: "If anyone expounds Judaism to you, do not listen. It is better to hear Christianity from a circumcised man than Judaism from an uncircumcised one" (To the Philadelphians 6.1). (3) Jewish followers of Jesus who insisted gentile believers become Jews first, like the group Paul fought in Galatians. (4) A mainly spiritual statement that the true people of God are those loyal to the Messiah, whatever their background. John Marshall and others stress that John never uses the word "Christian" and seems to think of himself and his churches as the faithful core of Israel. That makes this an argument inside a family about the family name, not an attack on Jews from outside.

Partly. The people were real, and so was the conflict. But the pattern also sets up one of Revelation's biggest themes: the true and the counterfeit. Jesus introduces himself to Philadelphia as "the Holy One, the True One" (3:7) and to Laodicea as "the faithful and true witness" (3:14), just before exposing false claims. Later the book is full of fakes: a beast with a death-wound that "was healed" like the slain Lamb (13:3), a second beast with "two horns like a lamb" that "spoke like a dragon" (13:11), a "false prophet" (16:13), a mark that copies God's seal, and a prostitute city that copies the bride. The beast wears "names that insulted God" (13:1), the divine titles emperors claimed: "Lord," "Savior," "Son of God." The local fakes in the letters are small versions of the great imperial fake. And the people with "no lie in their mouths" (14:5) stand opposite the "liars" left outside the city (21:8; 22:15).

sections.b: "Synagogue of Satan" has been taken out of context to justify hatred of Jews, from medieval sermons to modern hate groups that use it as a slogan. That use ignores that John was Jewish, that he names the twelve tribes on the gates of the New Jerusalem (21:12), and that his complaint is about specific local accusers in two cities. Most Christian traditions today explicitly reject reading these verses as a judgment on the Jewish people.

common: Real local opponents in the synagogues of Smyrna and Philadelphia, whose claim to the name John denies because they opposed the Messiah and his people.
False apostles and prophets were traveling teachers whom the churches were expected to test.
uncommon: Gentile Judaizers claiming Jewish status (Frankfurter).
Jewish-Christian teachers requiring gentiles to become Jews.
Historicist: nominal Christians or a church claiming to be the true Israel without its faith.
Replacement reading: the church is now the only "true Jews." Many object that John's point is loyalty, not ethnic replacement.

claude.title: Names you claim and names you are given
claude.body: My reading: the seven letters are a lesson in naming. People in them name themselves: apostles, Jews, a prophet, rich, alive (3:1, "you have a name that you are alive"; the Greek is literally "a name"). Jesus answers each self-given name by naming himself truly (each letter opens with one of his titles) and by promising names that only he can give: "a new name written on" a white stone "that no one knows except the one who receives it" (2:17), and "my God's name, the name of the city of my God... and my own new name" (3:12). In a world where a forged citizenship could cost your head, John's churches are told that the only identity that will stand on the last day is the one written by Jesus "in the book of life" (3:5). The beast tries the same thing on a world scale: it names itself with God's titles (13:1) and writes its own name on people (13:17). The question for every reader is not "What do I call myself?" but "Whose name is written on me?"
